AUTOMOBILES-ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one member of parliament who represents a constituency where the automobile industry plays such a great part in the economic life of the community, I welcome the action announced by the Prime Minister this morning. I may say to him that in announcing the commissioner, Professor Vincent Bladen, that gentleman has a qualification which I am sure the Prime Minister was not aware of, and I am sure if he had been aware of it he would not think the qualifications were as deserved as he and I both believe they are; and that is that Professor Bladen is an old professor of mine, as he is of the Minister of Finance. That, of course, will ease the blow a little in the Prime Minister's eyes, when he realizes that the Minister of Finance was taught some of his basic economics by Professor Bladen.
I had anticipated that the commission to be appointed by the government to look into the automobile industry would have been composed of more than one commissioner. I had anticipated there would be several commissioners so that various groups in the country would have been represented, including labour, management, the consumer and the state. However, the government has decided to appoint a single commissioner. I cannot speak too highly of his qualifications.
The problem facing the industry, however, as I am sure the Prime Minister will recognize, is of such a nature as not to be resolved merely by this study. I hope the inquiry will be prosecuted with dispatch, so the government will be enabled to reach conclusions which will improve the condition in that industry and increase the opportunity for employment. Meanwhile, however, the government, it seems to me, is not absolved from taking corrective measures

subtopic: AUTOMOBILES-ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext: I thought we had agreed on this, Mr. Speaker. I can say to the Prime Minister that the community from which I come in particular received the decision to appoint such a commission with understanding. We sincerely hope that the inquiry will be thorough and that it will be done quickly, because so much depends on it. The people of Windsor, so many thousands of whom are out of work, join me in thanking the Prime Minister for making this announcement today.

subtopic: AUTOMOBILES-ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad the Prime Minister has gone forward with the appointment of a commissioner to act as a royal commission to inquire into the automobile industry. This has been an industry of very great importance to Canada, but in recent years there has been evidence of difficulty in it. We think the scope of the inquiry set forth by the Prime Minister is important in so far it goes, but I should like to have had the Prime Minister spell out the terms of reference a little more adequately to make certain that the royal commission would inquire into all problems with regard to automation and into the field of management, and not a onesided inquiry into the labour unions.
I think it is a mistake to load this whole burden on one man. I believe the royal commission would be more effective if there were a number of commissioners, representative of the main economic groups interested in this industry, rather than putting the responsibility for report and decision on one man. I have another reason for advocating this proposition, Mr. Speaker. Although we in the C.C.F. acknowledge the outstanding qualities of Professor Bladen, nevertheless we believe that he is something of a small "c" conservative in his economic outlook. The commission could well have used additional personnel which would give it something of a broader outlook.
This is an important commission. We look forward to an early report. Newspapers have been saying the report will be in by the end of this year. I would ask the Prime Minister, if he cares to comment, whether he feels an inquiry of this scope may be completed by the end of this year so that action where desirable may be taken.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: AUTOMOBILES-ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, all I can say is this. We felt that if we had appointed several commissioners the period within which the report would ultimately be made would be somewhat longer than it would take one man to discharge this responsibility. As a matter of fact, on other occasions I have heard criticisms that royal commissions were too large in number, but it has always been so. Whatever you do there will always be criticism.

Mr. Speaker, I do not believe that this proposal can be taken seriously. It would obviously be impractical to try to bring together the heads of government of all the members of the United Nations during the general assembly, which is, as I understand it, what the Soviet proposal

amounts to. In effect this is simply another refusal on the part of the Soviet government to resume the disarmament negotiations which they broke off some weeks ago. It appears to be an attempt to undermine the western initiative in calling a meeting of the disarmament commission, which Canada and others have proposed in an effort to bring about a resumption of negotiations. Of course the Soviet authorities would not wish to put themselves in the position of flatly refusing to resume negotiations, and they have therefore, I would suggest, attempted to disguise what is in fact a refusal by putting forward this plainly impractical suggestion.

speechtext: I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, August 1, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-79, to provide for the recognition and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms -Mr. Diefenbaker-Mr. Flynn in the chair.
(Translation):

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just before we adjourned last night, I was trying to bring out the very restricted scope of this bill of rights, and I gave some illustrations from every day life with regard, for instance, to racial discrimination, freedom of religion, and the refusal to grant the services of an interpreter, in order to establish that in cases such as these, which might come up tomorrow, the bill would be entirely useless and would not provide any protection for the victim in the case.
At eleven o'clock last night I was stating that the bill which was submitted for first reading in this house on June 27 last, did not even mention the word "family". I notice that, among the various amendments inserted by the special committee, the word "family" is now mentioned in the preamble. And if hon. members will refer to the report of proceedings in committee, I hope we will be given credit, not only for urging the addition of a preamble but for calling the government's attention, by means of our various amendments, to the significance of the family in Canadian life.
Unfortunately, those amendments were rejected. Knowing as we do that a preamble is purely explanatory in nature, we may, this time tell the government how surprised and disappointed we are to see that the bill has come back without containing a reaffirmation of family rights, of family security and of the safeguard of the essential role still being played by the family in our society.
The Minister of Justice told us last night that he hoped to give this bill a very practical form so that it might be mounted on walls of homes and schools and in public places. That is fine. But it is not a calendar that we want, but a bill of rights, an efficient legislation and we want that legislation to recognize what the highest values in Canadian life are in this year 1960. Personally, I believe that the rights of the family rank first in this respect.
As a matter of fact, what are we doing here, we members of this house who are so proud of the prestige which is attached to

that title? As legislators, our role consists in nothing less than preparing for those who will come after us an improved pattern of life in which our children's personality will be allowed to develop completely. I also must point out that human rights and fundamental freedoms are not something static, but something which develops along with our society.
When we go over the list of rights and fundamental freedoms incorporated in Bill C-79, we note that most of them are rights that have been enjoyed for centuries. But life has changed in the meantime, and we should like to have a bill of rights that would recognize and state the highest values of this society of ours in this year 1960.
Mr. Chairman, I submit that, if we, in the opposition, had not insisted on the introduction in committee of various amendments relating to family rights, we would have been untrue to our political tradition. And if, at this stage, we were not again urging the introduction of amendments relating to family rights, I submit that we would be heedless of our political mission because, from time immemorial, the Liberal party's legislation has been focused upon recognition of family rights, and for all the social security laws we enjoy today we are indebted to the Liberal governments that came before the present government.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word only about the reference to the name of God in the bill now submitted to us with amendments. There was no such reference in the bill introduced on July 27.
In a preamble which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) submitted to our consideration in committee, there was reference to "spiritual values". I should like particularly to associate the names of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), and of the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion) to those of all other members of the committee who were successful in having the name of God included in the present bill.
Let me quote here a few lines of the remarks made in committee, on Friday, July 29, by the hon. member for Essex East:
(Text):
I agree with the minister fully, as every member of this committee does, that we would not want to put anything in a Canadian bill of rights that would be offensive to any religious denomination in our country; to Christians, to Jews, to Moslems, or to any other religious body which recognizes the existence of God. We are a country made up for the most part of religious-minded people. The majority of our people are Christians, but we have a very important and respectful group of Jewish citizens who subscribe to their faith, and we would not want, I am sure, any of us, to incorporate here anything that would
Human Rights
be offensive to them. But, it would seem to me, and I am open to correction, that in a bill of rights entertained and introduced by a country composed as we are of people who acknowledge the existence of God we should not hesitate to confirm that fact in some way in this preamble. In the preamble which I put forward reference to God is made twice-in the beginning and in the final paragraph.
An examination of other charters of human freedom, particularly the peoples charter, discloses that reference is made to God.
One of the basic differences between our free society and communism, the Soviet union totalitarian countries based upon dialectical materialism, is that religion itself and the existence of God are denied. For them. God does not exist and religion is regarded by this group as an opiate to hold down the progress of human beings. We make much of this fact in our ideological ideas. I believe we ought seriously to give recognition to this fact in this preamble.

Now, Mr. Chairman, I move on to another angle. Parliament has before it today a bill of rights, but no good reason has yet been given to us why the bill of rights which we are about to adopt should not apply in wartime as well as in peacetime.
The Prime Minister has told us that this bill is a first step only and that, at another session, the War Measures Act would be amended. I believe that if the matter of this bill of rights, both in peacetime and in wartime, had been submitted to us, such experts as university professors and all those who were heard in the committee could have expressed their views on this matter. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have before us a bill of vital importance. In my opinion it solemnly establishes a charter which should be the cornerstone of any true democracy.
In a book entitled "Democracy", Georges Budeau, professor of the faculty of law, in Paris, wrote at the beginning of his book the following:
In theory and in fact, democracy is indissolubly related to the idea of liberty. Its simplest as well as its truest definition, that is government of the people by the people, attains its true meaning only because it excludes any power proceeding from an authority other than the people. Therefore, democracy is first and foremost a system of government which strives to include liberty ini the political relation, that is, in the relation between orders and obedience which are inherent in any politically organized society. Authority doubtless remains to a mixed degree so that, based as it is on the acceptance of those who are subject to it, it nevertheless remains consistent with their liberty.
The relationship between the freedom of man and the authority of the state, the limits within which the governors and the governed may carry out their activities, this is exactly what this bill attempts to define.
This charter is the outcome of views long held by the Prime Minister. It was born of the firm and determined will to provide every Canadian citizen with the means of forming, developing and expressing himself and of playing, in his country's service, the part assigned to him by society.
Such is the basic characteristic of this bill. Therein lies its loftiness and its beauty. That is why the right hon. Prime Minister deserves the highest praise and congratulations for having introduced it in this house.
Mr. Chairman, before submitting this charter to the house for final discussion and adoption, the Prime Minister felt it should first be reviewed by a special committee. Looking at the background of the various members of that committee, one is struck by its variety and scope. Indeed, the 15 Canadians in that committee were of nine or ten different nationalities.
I must recognize, Mr. Chairman, that I have seldom witnessed in that kind of committee such a frank and objective discussion of each and every clause of the bill by such diverse people. It made me realize how people
Human Rights
so different and of such various origins can work in harmony.

And why did this happen? Simply because every member of the committee without any exception was conscious of the fact that he was taking part in a momentous event, in a wonderful guarantee for the future, and every one was firmly determined to do all that is humanly possible to provide our country with a charter affording the possibility of evolving true Canadian unity, based on harmony among the various racial groups and good will among the people of various extractions that make up the Canadian nation.

There, Mr. Chairman, you have, in my opinion, one of the greatest accomplishments of which Canada can rightly be proud. There you have, once again, the first great advantage of this bill which, in my opinion, has already brought about an achievement of the greatest importance.
And here, I recall what the Prime Minister said, when introducing the bill around July 10, I believe, and I quote from Le Devoir of July 12:
All my life I have been waiting for that day when there would emerge in this country a Cana-dianism proud of its ancestry, which would allow every Canadian openly to express his national pride. We all know that, in the past, distinctions have existed in our minds. I have known here, these last few days, an unforgettable feeling, the feeling that we are building within our nation a Canadianism that is common to all provinces.
And I believe I may add that this feeling, each one of us felt it that day.
Mr. Chairman, yesterday I heard the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) say that in his opinion-which I believe he shares with the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue)-the bill in its present wording is very different from the original bill introduced in the house by the Prime Minister.
Evidently, if the Prime Minister saw fit to send it to a special committee, it is precisely because he wanted to show the house just how anxious he was to see that that charter was as complete and as perfect as any human document can be.

Human Rights
And that gesture, one of modesty, indicating how solicitous he is to respect the members of this house and their opinions is, to my mind, an additional example which throws into strong relief the Prime Minister's character and shows to what extent he was adverse to making this bill his own personal handiwork but wanted instead to make it the business of all Canadians, so that all of them might rejoice in having such a bill of rights as an expression of their own aspirations.
When comparing those texts-the original and the present one-we obviously note rather marked differences. But to my mind, those differences proceed from an identical substance, the substance already contained in the original bill, and from the originating principle according to which, as we can read in the preamble, clear and practical recognition must be given to the spiritual and moral values which characterize our country, which must always be at the root of our legislation and which are as the distinctive trait which separate us from communism, where God and all spiritual values are subordinate to the most depressing and abject materialism. It can therefore be said, Mr. Chairman, that, on the whole, the Prime Minister's project gives spiritual values a priority over material values. That is its essential feature. The Prime Minister therefore resorted to a committee. The members of that committee gave all the assistance they could. And I want to repeat that it was because of a spirit of harmony, because of a spirit of agreement and good understanding that this bill has become the result of teamwork, the fruit of each and every member's thoughts, without exception. The preamble itself merely sets out in eloquent terms the source from which human rights and freedom flow.
The Leader of the Opposition told us last night that he would have preferred a bill of rights endorsed by all the provinces and taking the form of a constitutional amendment. To show that agreement by all provinces was possible, he recalled words spoken by Mr. Lesage during the recent federal-provincial conference.
When the bill was introduced in 1958 and on various occasions since, the Prime Minister of Canada invariably evinced his concern to confine himself to human rights and freedoms in their relation to the federal state. In this, he was perfectly right. Would it not be inconsistent, Mr. Chairman, and even ineon-
[Mr. Dorion.j
ceivable, that a bill of rights should, by itself, and by the scope of the powers it is supposed to embrace, impinge upon the provincial constitutional rights likewise designed to protect man within the society in which he is called upon to live and develop?
Was that not indeed, and until very recently, the opinion of the Leader of the Opposition, when, in 1948 at the United Nations he referred to the particular circumstances in which we live here in Canada, and clearly stated his wish to respect those particular conditions? And I quote what he said in 1948 during the debate at the United Nations. My quotation is from the magazine Relations for November 1958:
(Text):
I wish to make it clear here, that, in regard to any rights that are defined in this document-
(Translation):
Speaking about the universal bill of rights. (Text):
-the federal government of Canada does not intend to invade other rights which are also important to the people of Canada. By this I mean the rights of the provinces under our federal constitution. We believe that the rights set forth in this declaration are operated and well protected in Canada. We shall continue to develop and maintain these rights, but we shall do so within the framework of our constitution which assigns jurisdiction in regard to a number of important questions to the legislatures of our provinces.
(Translation):
Of course, I am not trying to blame the Leader of the Opposition. I am merely noting that his attitude had varied since the day when Mr. Lesage, last July, that is quite recently, at the federal-provincial conference where the agenda made no reference to the problem, suddenly made a statement to the effect that he was prepared to cooperate in drafting a national bill of rights. At that time, Mr. Chairman, the whole question had been debated in the house and the bill had gone through second reading. It had been submitted to a committee whose task was necessarily restricted by its terms of reference and also by the fact that, prior to second reading, government supporters and members of the official opposition had all voted against amending the constitution after consultation with the provinces.
Such were the circumstances at the time of Mr. Lesage's statement. We could not properly, logically and legally modify our terms of reference or the authorization granted us by parliament, for we would have been going against the will of parliament and against the basic principles of

sound democracy. Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, last January the Quebec legislature had unanimously passed a resolution. I must say that a number of persons were on hand who are now members of the cabinet of Mr. Le-sage. As I say, the legislature had passed a resolution clearly indicating its will, or the will of the province of Quebec as represented by the legislature, not to share in a bill of rights. In that connection, I should like to quote from an article by the Quebec correspondent of La Presse, published on February 18, 1960:
Yesterday the legislative assembly unanimously took position on the bill of rights which Prime Minister Diefenbaker is seeking to put through the Canadian House of Commons.
Carried was a motion proclaiming that the proposed federal legislation should in no way, whether directly or indirectly, encroach upon the recognized exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces, under the British North America Act.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I think we can say without boasting that one of our first concerns, of myself and of all the members of the committee-and I commend them for it -was precisely to scrutinize the bill scrupulously, to make sure it contained nothing that might encroach on provincial rights. That, I may say was as a leitmotiv throughout our discussions. That is precisely why, in the preamble to the bill, it is very definitely and very clearly stated that the legislator, or the federal parliament, has no desire to interfere with the rights, privileges and freedoms which are recognized as belonging to the provinces. I am not criticizing Mr. Lesage for his attitude, though I think it is at variance with the will of the Quebec legislature. I am merely trying to deal with the objections which have been raised at this stage in the proceedings.
And I will add this: there is no sign that the legislature has changed its mind in spite of the premier's opinion because the matter is too serious, too important, too vital for the group that the province of Quebec is responsible for protecting, or for us to agree perfunctorily to some improvised statement, a statement which has not previously been submitted to public bodies, to various associations and still less to the legislature itself.
On that point, may I recall this: in the Canadian Bar Review, there is an article by Mr. Louis-Philippe Pigeon, and I must say, incidentally, that this article had impressed me enough to impel me to seek a meeting with Mr. Pigeon, who is a professor at Laval University, in order to discuss with him the 79951-0-467
Human Rights
various objections he had to this bill of rights. The outcome of that meeting was a letter which I showed to some members of the committee, in which Mr. Pigeon was saying that the wording should be clarified so as to remove any uncertainty, any ambiguity as to the legislator's intent to limit the application of the bill to such human rights as come under the powers and rights of the federal state.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, I must add that Mr. Pigeon-and I say this to correct the impression which my good friend from Maison-neuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) might have left-Mr. Pigeon and others in the province of Quebec were invited to attend the committee meetings, but for various reasons they did not show up. I must add at once-[DOT] again to correct another statement made by my excellent friend-that at least three professors from the province of Quebec expressed their views before the committee.
In French only.

Now let me adduce a further argument which, in my opinion necessarily came to our minds when the suggestion was made to adjourn our discussion indefinitely until such time as Mr. Lesage was able to express with clarity and precision-
Hear, hear.

I am not saying this in any disparaging sense and would not like hon. members to construe it so-I merely wish to say, in order to allow Mr. Lesage to tell us exactly to what extent he was prepared to work at the framing of a national bill of rights.
I believe this suggestion was premature because, in the province of Quebec-and I apologize to my colleagues of the other provinces if, for a moment I am considering the problem from this strictly provincial angle- we have a legislative system which is centered on the family, a legislative system in which the expression of civil rights is different from what it is elsewhere. And Heaven knows to what extent the French racial group in Canada has always considered, and still considers, that institution which is particular to it, this institution of civil law, as one of the most vital factors to its safeguard and its survival.
Mr. Chairman, a national bill of human rights in which the whole province would

Human Rights
be interested, a bill that would include the basic rights of the citizen as such and in his relations with his fellow citizens-which is civil law-would be of considerable impact on our civil code, on our particular institutions. Please note that I am against this wish. If unanimity can be logically achieved, I will say: so much the better for Canadian unity. But, unless and until I have been convinced that a national bill of human rights cannot in any way affect, say, the rights of a father with regard to his children, his relations with his children, which relations are now defined in the civil code, the husband and wife relationship, the husband's authority, paternal authority, the order of inheritance; as long as I have not been fully convinced that we can draft a text consonant with those basic institutions which are so dear to us, I say that a national bill of human rights must inspire us with the greatest caution. Therefore I repeat that must be so, as long as I have not been convinced that those basic institutions, which have guaranteed our survival, can be made to agree with the contents of a national bill of human rights.
Besides, Mr. Chairman, a look at history will show that I have just dealt with a prime concern of our group. As early as 1760, the first request made by our defeated leaders was the maintenance and preservation of our civil rights. In 1774, we were given a text whereby our group is assured preservation of its civil rights. In 1841, an attempt was made to unify Upper and Lower Canada by the Union act. What were the results? Exactly the opposite; moreover, it was under the Union act the two main pieces of legislation of the province of Quebec-the civil code and the code of civil procedure-were drafted.
Then, in 1867, when on the one hand the colonies of British extraction or of British allegiance agreed to include in the constitutional act of 1867 a provision which made uniform legislation possible, the province of Quebec demanded that an exception be made on her behalf. Why that exception, if not because the province foresaw a danger of absorption and assimilation. Is it possible through a mere statement made on the occasion of a conference here in Ottawa to agree to the solution of so serious a problem simply because the premier of Quebec-whom I respect-expressed a personal opinion that may have serious consequences? I do not say that a national bill

of human rights would be absolutely unacceptable. My purpose is simply and exclusively to show very clearly how very important it is not to accept such a statement inconsiderately and without giving the premier of Quebec and his colleagues an opportunity fully to realize the importance and implications of such action, so that we might in due course have a truly national bill of human rights, as a result of a genuine agreement entered into as a result of actual work, thinking and a profound certainty of not having interfered in any way with the inalienable rights which the province of Quebec is bound to preserve with such perseverance.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, the point was also made that we should have proceeded through an amendment to the constitution.
Well, sir, at this stage, with very definite opinions forcefully expressed by the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), leader of his group, to the effect that the time has come for Canada to have her own constitutional amending instruments, I think it would have been unthinkable for us to call upon Westminster or London to take a hand in making the wealth of our rights and freedoms accessible, so to speak, to all Canadians.
That, to my mind, is absolutely illogical. In my opinion, the right hon. Prime Minister was right in reminding us that the day we repatriate-some doubt has been expressed and with reason in connection with the word but, for lack of a better one we have to use it-that the day we repatriate our constitution, the day we find some specific way of doing so in such manner that it would not interfere with the fundamental rights of the two main racial groups which constitute this country, then we can think of amending the constitution and giving Canadian citizens a national bill of rights.
Mr. Chairman, I now want to say a word on the subject mentioned by my good friend the member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets), that is, family rights. I am prepared to believe that the hon. member raised the point quite honestly and without any ulterior electoral motive.
Never. Impossible.

Mr. Chairman, in this respect, it is rather surprising to note that a present

minister in Mr. Lesage's government, Mr. Lafrance, in a statement made in the Quebec legislature on January 19, 1960, asserted that under the constitution certain fundamental rights came under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial legislature, and that in those fundamental rights were precisely included family rights. This is what Mr. Lafrance said:
This house urges the provincial government to take all necessary action to introduce an act establishing the rights and freedoms of individuals and more especially those of the family-
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, Mr. Lafrance was entirely right.
With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer to Mr. Albert Sorel, a great French philosopher. According to Mr. Sorel, private law applies to all citizens from the time of their birth, through adolescence to majority, sanctions their marriage, certifies their death and throughout their life, regulates the right to work, to enter into contracts, to dispose of themselves and of their property.
A complete bill of human rights would necessarily have had the result of affecting the very root of civil rights, and more particularly, all institutions protecting the family.
Nothing comes closer to civil rights than this problem and if the committee did not agree to follow my good friend in this direction, it is exactly because, as I said earlier, we wanted to comply with the views of the legislature itself, with the views of his own friends, since we were warned in January or February not to infringe in any way upon the rights and powers of the province of Quebec nor of any other province in this country.

Mr. Chairman, I quite appreciate the intervention of the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and I 79951-0-467J

must say that, not only during the sittings of the committee but ever since I have been a member of this house, he has been so kind, gracious and courteous to me that very often I have felt embarrassed about it. I appreciate his behaviour very highly and I am glad of this occasion of saying so.
Mr. Chairman, in 1959, the Semaines sociales du Canada, an organization whose members meet each year for the study of social or sociological problems, met last year in Quebec city. The theme of their conference, or the main idea of their meeting, was a study of the mission and the rights of the family. In the opening speech, Rev. Father Richard Ares, chairman of the Semaines sociales du Canada, who is particularly known in Quebec sociological circles, stated the following, that I find at page 21 of the report:
In order to be still more practical and precise, I shall add this. I see only advantages in a bill of family rights which would be jointly and freely enforced by both levels of government that form our federal system and would later command the respect of each. Even if the statement were the work of a single level of government, I, for my part, hold the view that it should first be made by the government which is essentially responsible for matters relating to the family, that is, for us from the province, the Quebec government.
We have here a view which has the merit of having been expressed by one of our greatest sociologists in the province of Quebec, by a man who took the trouble to study constitutional problems and was a member of the Tremblay commission, recently referred to by Mr. Lesage, and therefore a man who, in dealing with such problems, does so as one who has gone deeply into the matter, and knows the subject from all angles, including the legal one.
So Rev. Father Ares tells us that the family comes within provincial jurisdiction. It is so true that, in the civil code there are at least four or five complete chapters dealing with the relationships between husband and wife, between father and children, between wife and children, between grandfather and grandchildren, about the order of inheritance, all of their problems that lie exclusively within provincial jurisdiction, because relationships between individuals are problems of private law. The matter goes so far that I should like to make my point clear by stating a concrete example. If a family wants to change its name, the authority which will allow it to do so, which is able to achieve that purpose, the only one that exists, is the

Human Rights
provincial legislature and not the federal government. In other words, if family rights such as they might be defined on the basis of suggestions put forward in the committee, are not mentioned in the present bill of rights, it is solely and exclusively out of respect for the clearly expressed will of members on both sides of the house not to interfere in a field which is outside our scope, as this would have been a violation of the constitution, of which we are the guardians and which is truly the cornerstone of Canadian unity.
Mr. Chairman, before closing my remarks, I again thank the hon. member for Essex East, and I would not want to take undue advantage of the kindness that is being shown to me.
In conclusion, may I say that here is a bill of rights that will be of considerable educational value for the Canadian people, for our children, for every province, because in future, we will have the solemn statement that here is the death knell of prejudices, to which all of us have been more or less subjected in the days of our youth and which still live in certain parts of Canada, prejudices whereby a person, because of the colour of his skin, is looked upon as a stranger, or gives the impression of somehow not belonging altogether to the human species.
The other day I had an opportunity of meeting the prime minister of the Congo. What pride I felt when I had the privilege of thanking him after a speech he made,-how proud I was to be able to quote section 1 of the bill of human rights which told him that here, in Canada, the skin, the colour, the religion, all those things are in no way a handicap to those who wish to live here in Canada, in this land blessed by God. He noticed the atmosphere of the country that was welcoming him, just as he noticed the relation of our culture with that of the Congo or the Congolese.
Mr. Chairman, this bill will have an educational value for our children, for the provinces and for all people in Canada; it will show mankind that, here in Canada, spiritual and moral values come first, that material values are subordinate to spiritual values and that our rights are established according to specific principles. Moreover, nationals of other countries who wish to work with us, to join their efforts and their strength with ours and thus to form with us the population of Canada,

will know where we stand and will feel that at last, on Canadian soil, they have found the land of freedom.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion) allow me to ask a question?
Yes.

Should some of the remarks of the member for Bellechasse be understood as an objection to the proposal made by the premier of Quebec to call a federal-provincial conference to consider together the possibility of adopting a bill of rights on a national scale a proposition which seems to have been endorsed by the Prime Minister of Canada?

My honourable colleague will find that I said nothing of the kind. All I said was that, to my mind, the question was premature because its consideration requires preliminary groundwork, and especially, a knowledge of the extent to which a national bill of rights might affect the fundamental rights of the province of Quebec.
May I put a supplementary question to the member for Bellechasse?
Yes.
Is this not the very purpose of the consultation and the conference that would be held in that connection?
He did not say so.

That was not my understanding. The reports I have seen may not be complete, but that was not what I gathered. But even if it were so, I fail to see how this bill could possibly stand in the way of that further consideration. On the contrary, in my opinion it represents a giant step towards the elimination of a difficulty comparable by nature to that suggested by the member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin).

The first thing I should like to do is express my appreciation for the privilege of serving on this committee. While the number of days during which the committee sat were comparatively few, considering the importance of the subject, the number of hours spent in an exhaustive study of submissions and the evidence of witnesses were many. Of all the committees on which I have had the honour to serve, the committee on the bill of rights was by far the most absorbing and interesting, and by and large its work was carried out in an atmosphere of

congenial friendliness, as was pointed out so eloquently by the hon. member for Belle-chasse, a very distinguished member of the committee.
I would also say that while the amendments put forward by the members of the opposition did not always secure the approval of the majority, nevertheless considerable progress was made, thanks to the co-operative attitude of the Minister of Justice and the capable chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Essex West, who conducted the meetings in a very fair and efficient manner. For all these reasons, not the least of which is the opportunity afforded to me of making a small contribution toward such a noble objective, I am glad this bill of rights was introduced this session, despite its many imperfections.
Having paid a well-earned compliment to the hon. member for Essex West it would be unfair if I did not mention the leadership given to the committee by the hon. member for Essex East, whose keen legal mind was a tower of strength in the committee's deliberations, the results of which are evident in the improvement of the bill. Thus, having laced the sage man of the west with the wise man of the east, I express the sincere hope that once passed this bill will not be forgotten and left in its present form, even its amended form, but that the Prime Minister will ensure that it is discussed with all the provinces with the end in view that a real Canadian bill of rights, which would stand up in all conditions, in all circumstances and in all the provinces may be enacted at the earliest possible moment.
During the committee hearings we heard evidence from a number of organizations and several distinguished individual experts whose opinions were carefully weighed and from which we in the opposition learned much. This was helpful in bringing in our amendments. Unfortunately, many of our 20-odd amendments, most of which were based on the recommendations of the witnesses and of such historic documents as the United Nations declaration of human rights and the United States bill of rights, were rejected, in my view on insufficient legislative grounds, with the result that opportunities of particularizing the rights to be protected were lost.
However, the minister did accept the principle of a preamble, which we had advocated from the beginning. This, incidentally, was first suggested by the Leader of the Opposition. Several members of the committee on both sides proposed preambles, all of which contained meritorious ideas and phraseology, in an attempt to make our bill of rights a memorable document. The preamble which
Human Rights
was finally adopted was really a product of the whole committee, despite press reports which indicated that it was the brain child of the Minister of Justice. The preamble really gives dignity to the document, which is largely legalistic and skimpy in its specification of the rights contained in it. My suggested preamble was as follows:
In recognition that the Canadian people believe in the dignity of man and are composed of many races and religious beliefs, the parliament of Canada hereby declares and reaffirms the people's fundamental liberty to work and to worship his God to the satisfaction of his conscience and Her Majesty, the Queen, with the advice and consent of the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows-
However, the one which was finally adopted was a much better introduction to the bill. A good job was done on the preamble.
I have indicated that the minister did accept some of our amendments, one of which, incidentally, is the right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty. This is one of the amendments I was ready to introduce when the minister announced that he had such an amendment already in mind, for which I congratulated the minister on his foresight and almost clairvoyant perception.
Another amendment which I proposed in committee and which the minister accepted was that no persons should be deprived of the right to reasonable bail without just cause. Incidentally, this clause is part of the United States bill of rights, which prescribes that excessive bail should not be required. I think the minister was wise in accepting this amendment, which undoubtedly gives clause 2 more substance.
What I could not appreciate was the minister's reluctance to spelling out specific provisions in language easy for everyone to understand, instead of leaving meanings up in the air and making provision by inference. Provision by inference is not good enough in a bill of rights for the people of Canada.
With this truism in mind the Liberal members of the committee moved a number of amendments the effect of which would have been to make the bill more specific and more meaningful to the general public as well as to the courts. At least one of these was anticipated and, as I indicated earlier, was introduced by the minister himself before we moved to fill the gap. Others were accepted on our motion. Too many, however, were rejected by the minister and voted down by the majority of the committee.
It is easy to find important examples to illustrate my point. I shall, however, refer to one about which I feel particularly strongly. Last Thursday afternoon I moved in the

Human Rights
committee that the following provision be added to clause 2 as it then stood:
The right of the individual to earn a living and to free choice of employment, to just and favourable conditions of work, and to protection against unemployment.
This amendment like many others was rejected at least partially on the ground that it is now embraced, not separately and individually but in the sum total of the bill as it now is before the committee of the whole house. Further, in this particular rejection the Minister of Justice clarified the government's position as being that this amendment was nothing more than the statement of an objective the realization of which would require specific measures. I am referring to what the minister said as reported in the proceedings and minutes of the committee, on page 663. He went on to say that we already have such a measure on the statute books, the Unemployment Insurance Act. There are, of course, others.
This is the very point I made in moving the amendment when I said, as reported in the minutes on page 661:
-the right which is envisioned-has been generally recognized in Canada during most of this century.
I might, had I not wanted to avoid verbosity-and I am not prone to speaking at length at any time-have gone into detail to show that there was nothing in the proposed amendment which was inconsistent with the general statement of the present clause 1. The rights referred to may be only objectives for some countries of the world, as the minister argued. They are, however, generally recognized rights in Canada, and the minister chose to ignore the need for the classification of these rights.
My proposed amendment to the effect that the Minister of Justice shall report legislative inconsistencies to an appropriate standing committee of the House of Commons, and that all petitions of citizens who feel that their rights had been infringed be referred to that committee, was rejected. In view of the minister's reply that there is not now such a committee, and in view of the amendment now incorporated in clause 3 providing that the minister shall report inconsistencies to the house, I propose at the beginning of the next session of this parliament to move the establishment of a standing committee on human rights and fundamental freedoms.
Anyone who cares to do so can learn of the effectiveness of the New Zealand public petitions committee. I addressed myself to that subject in the debate on second reading of this bill. The Prime Minister in closing that debate almost seconded my proposal
[Mr. Badanai.l
to establish a similar committee in this parliament which, after all, should not lag far behind the younger parliaments of the commonwealth in protecting the rights of its citizens. On second reading of the bill, as reported at page 5684 of Hansard of July 4, I made the following suggestion:
I suggest the establishment of an effective public petitions committee similar to that which has been set up in New Zealand. Perhaps such a committee could be established in the other place; no more trustworthy agency to discharge the duties of such a committee could be found than that august body, the Canadian Senate.
Some may forget what the Prime Minister said on July 7, as reported at page 5948 of Hansard:
When it is suggested that there should be a scrutiny committee, may I say that that suggestion which I have made on other occasions is one that deserves the fullest consideration and no doubt it will be among those things which will be considered and deliberated upon in the days to come.
Those were the words of the Prime Minister. I think any legislative or other inconsistencies reported to the house by the Minister of Justice might well be referred to a standing committee on human rights and fundamental freedoms. Likewise, all petitions to be based on the Canadian bill of rights should be referred to such a committee. It should then classify and condense the petitions in such form and manner as might appear best suited to convey to the house all requisite information respecting their contents. The committee should have power to sit at any time, to send for papers and persons, but not for ministers; the place for ministers to argue is in the house. The committee should be assisted and advised in its work by a competent parliamentary official such as the parliamentary counsel.

Mr. Chairman, as I observe that you are rising to call it one o'clock may I ask if the committee would give unanimous consent to allow the hon. gentleman to finish his remarks? Perhaps we could also continue through the lunch hour.
Agreed.

I thank the committee, Mr. Chairman. To continue, the committee should

With regard to petitions it should be able to recommend that petitions (a) be rejected; or (b) be referred by the House of Commons to the government for (1) consideration, (2) favourable consideration and (3) granting in whole or in part; or (c) the committee might recommend that the petitioners take action in the courts.
