speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2 p.m.

In speaking on this bill on July 4, on second reading, as reported in Hansard, starting at page 5695, I attempted to set out some of the difficulties that were apparent to me and some of the problems that this bill engendered; but I concluded my remarks by suggesting that even if there were imperfections in the bill it went a long way toward establishing in Canada basic rights and fundamental freedoms, and I suggested that we should adopt the measure so that we might place upon the statute books of this country those things that we as Canadian people have enjoyed as part of our way of life.
It is true that there are uncertainties in the bill; there are difficulties arising out of Canada's constitutional set-up, but uncertainties applied to the British North America Act, and had our forefathers at the time of confederation allowed those uncertainties and difficulties to stand in the way we would not have the Dominion of Canada today. The truth of that statement lies in the fact that almost 200 cases have arisen over the interpretation of the British North America Act, and over 100 have gone to the privy council
Human Rights
for adjudication. I see no reason for changing the opinion I expressed on that previous occasion, but after having had an opportunity to serve on the committee I think I have a better appreciation of the problems and difficulties connected with the bill as well as the advantages and the help that it will provide for all Canadians.
First of all I wish to thank the hon. member for Essex West, who was chairman of that committee. He did a remarkable job, considering that he had a very diversified class to work with. I want to thank also the members of the committee, and I have particular thanks and praise for the hon. member for Bellechasse and also the hon. member for Essex East. I did not agree with him on many occasions, but I think every member of the committee had a keen appreciation of the other person's point of view, and out of the deliberations has come the bill now before us. At this time I want to thank the Prime Minister for introducing a bill which is so important to the people of this country.
In speaking on this bill yesterday the Leader of the Opposition had some criticisms to offer, and I want to refer to some of those criticisms. The first criticism had to do with the timing of the bill. He criticized the Prime Minister for, after having introduced the bill in 1958, delaying its introduction this year until July 1. I should like to refer the Leader of the Opposition-and I do this kindly, without any unjust criticism-to several of the briefs submitted to the special committee and some of the observations made therein by those who presented the briefs. I want to refer to the brief of the congress of labour, in which they said they had been trying since 1947 to have a bill of rights introduced in Canada. I refer io the brief of the associated civil liberties committee, and they also refer to 1947. Therefore I feel that the criticism of the Leader of the Opposition as to timing is most unjust and most unkind.
I should like to place on the record an observation made in one of the briefs, which appears in the committee record. I refer to the brief of the seventh day adventists, at page 71:
The passage of this measure will mark an historic and significant milestone for this country in its quest for freedom and peace under the rule of law.
The leader of the C.C.F. party also had some criticisms regarding the proposed bill, and although he was a member of that committee -and I say this not unkindly-his contribution to the deliberations did not measure up to the contribution made by the other members. In this connection I want to place on

Human Rights
record my appreciation of the contribution made by the members of the official opposition. On all occasions they co-operated with the steering committee and with the committee itself in its deliberations.
The Leader of the Opposition referred to the observations of Professor Scott in which he was rather critical of the bill; but I would point out to him that Professor Scott, although critical of the bill, did not bring to the committee, in my opinion at least, any constructive proposals. His only proposal was in the form of a constitutional amendment. His proposed amendment was to the effect that the parliament of Canada should surrender part of its sovereignty; in other words, it should place beyond itself the right to amend its own constitution, the right to have any power over its own institutions.
I point out to the leader of the C.C.F. party that this proposal was not concurred in by A. N. Carter, Q.C., a distinguished New Brunswick lawyer. In an article in the Canadian Bar Review, which is also part of the record of the committee, he said that taking that step would result in placing the Canadian constitution farther away from the Canadian people and the Canadian parliament.
The same opinion as to a constitutional amendment was introduced by Dr. Forsey, who appeared with the Canadian Labour Congress delegation. He agreed with Professor Scott that an amendment to the constitution should be made in order that Canada could no longer change its constitution so as to interfere with any fundamental rights and freedoms previously established.
I suggest that is not the proper approach to this matter and is a regressive step. The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont, speaking in the house this morning, pointed out that the bill of rights does not in express terms, except in the preamble, deal with family life. I suggest to him, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Belle-chasse, that the rights of the family are included in the individual rights set out in the bill. The bill of rights cannot affect a unit or a group but must apply to that group through the individuals comprising it. I suggest that in the personal freedoms set out in the bill we have looked after and protected the family group.
What were some of the criticisms levelled at the proposed bill before the committee? I suggested in my previous remarks and I suggested in the committee that the bill is not perfect, but I submit that it deals only with those matters within the legislative jurisdiction of the federal government and for the present that is all we can expect. We have heard a great deal about the possibility of an amendment to the constitution in consultation with

the provinces. I suggest to the committee that that is a far cry from actual consent, and it was submitted by various witnesses before the committee that such consent would not be forthcoming, at the present time. It is very significant, as was pointed out in the committee, that this new approach was made in the closing days of the committee's deliberations.
There has been some criticism that the bill infringes on provincial rights. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this fear has been banished by the address of the hon. member for Bellechasse, supported as it was by the evidence of the various witnesses before the committee. I need only refer to the evidence of Professor Scott and Professor Bowker, who said there was no infringement of provincial rights. The committee on civil liberties, the Canadian Labour Congress and even Dr. Forsey said that the bill in its present form did not infringe or attempt to infringe upon any provincial matter. I would also refer the committee to the evidence given by Dr. Maxwell Cohen of McGill University, as reported at page 373 of the evidence.
As I intimated before, it was proposed in the closing days of the committee's deliberations that the matter should be postponed and the provinces should be consulted. That was not the attitude of the Canadian Labour Congress. As found on page 226 of the evidence they say that we should pass the present bill, that it will be a step in the right direction, and then at the proper time and place we should discuss with the provinces those amendments necessary to make our constitution wholly Canadian and our bill of rights wholly national.
We also have the statement of Professor Lower at page 323 of the evidence, that in the present state of the country the provinces would not consent. I assume that the professor made that statement with a keen appreciation of the problems involved. We also have the evidence given by Professor Bowker that he was opposed to a constitutional amendment.
These are some of the criticisms that have been raised with respect to the bill. There has also been some talk in the past about sending the bill to the Supreme Court of Canada by way of a reference in order to determine its validity. That suggestion has been more or less dispelled by the evidence given in the committee. I refer to the brief of the Canadian Labour Congress and the evidence of Professor Bowker and others who were opposed to such a procedure. The consensus of all the witnesses was that this bill should be passed and then, as developments

occurred, the necessary changes could be made or a reference then made to the Supreme Court.
We are not dealing here with a subject matter than can be pigeonholed and categorically defined. We are dealing with human rights. We are dealing with the play and interplay of human relations on human beings, and we can only legislate in that field with an appreciation and an understanding of all the prolbems that arise from that relationship. There are no absolute rights when dealing with human beings. Those freedoms set out in the bill are relative freedoms. They are, as one of the witnesses before the committee pointed out, more "values" than freedoms. Freedom is not licence. It is freedom under rule of law; it is freedom under recognized customs of society, laws that we ourselves have established, and it is within and under these laws that we must conduct our human relations.
We in Canada enjoy freedoms brought to this country from two great bodies of law, the common law of England and the Roman law in so far as it has been adapted as part of the civil code. It is in the development of that law, the interrelation of the groups with each other, that we make progress. Progress, after all, is only continual adaptation to an ever-changing environment. Macaulay in his essay "The History of the Revolution" says:
The history of England is emphatically the history of progress. It is the history of a constant movement of the public mind, of a constant change in the constitution of a great society.
Dicey and other writers of the eighteenth century could and did write of the sovereignty of parliament and the rule of law as the cardinal features of the English constitution. However, over the intervening years there has been a gradual change, as Sir Alfred Denning points out in his book "The Changing Law", at page 1:
In legal theory parliament is still sovereign, and we still claim to be under the rule of law; but anxiety is raised in many quarters by the growing powers of the executive. The change has no doubt been forced upon us by circumstances. You cannot fight great wars except by giving your leaders power to make great decisions and to translate them into immediate action. You cannot safeguard your currency and trade in a competitive world except by strict control over exchange, and over exports and imports. You cannot ensure fair distribution of necessaries which are in short supply except by a system of rationing. You cannot nationalize essential industries except by putting them under the general direction of the government. All this involves the entrusting of great powers to the executive; and the powers, once given, are apt to continue indefinitely. Some, indeed, have been made permanent; and others cannot be retracted.
If that is a true indication of our present state in Canada, I suggest to the members of
79951-0-468
Human Rights
this committee that this bill of rights will serve as a curb on the growing power of the executive. After referring to the power of the executive, in the same book at page 2, the author refers to Westminster hall and to the power and place that should be occupied by the courts. He says:
Such memories will bring back to you some of the great constitutional issues which have been decided by the English people. But you should also remember that, in this hall for nigh on 700 years, the judges of England laid down the common law which precisely defined the rights of the individual and made the life and liberty of every law-abiding citizen secure from injury on the part of others or of the state. Here sat the judges of England right from the days of King Henry II in 1189 till the year 1873 when the courts were moved to their present situation in the Strand. The principles laid down by them have sunk deep into the mind of the nation and have been more powerful than anything else in creating the spirit of the British constitution. If you reflect on all this in that hall, so strong and so well balanced, so built as if for all time, you will get a sense of wonderful history, and with it a knowledge that the English people-and their cousins throughout the British commonwealth-are heirs of a spiritual worth which is a greater power in the world than armies or navies or atomic bombs.
I quoted that part to show this is something that is inbred in every true Canadian. I ask that at this time we keep this basic concept of freedom in mind in our examination of this bill. The bill might not be all we want, but I submit that it is a step in the right direction, and as long as the people of this country are conscious of their rights and freedoms and are determined to retain and to improve those freedoms, we are safe from intrusions and there will forever remain in the minds of Canadians a desire for those things which have been set out in this bill of rights. The criticism that it does not go far enough in some respects, that it is uncertain in some respects, that in one or more aspects it might infringe on some of the powers now held by the provinces, in my opinion should not be valid reasons for withholding passage of this bill.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say, first of all, how grateful I am for the privilege of having been a member of the special committee on the bill of rights. I came from that committee with a much clearer conception of what the problems are, and of the importance of a bill of rights to the Canadian people. I am not a lawyer, and I speak as a layman. As a result of being a member of that committee I was able to see the bill of rights in broader view than I had before going into the committee.
I am not, Mr. Chairman, going to make any very extended remarks at this time, as I shall be following with a great deal of interest some of the clauses which will come

Human Rights
before the committee this afternoon. However, since I did not speak on either of the earlier occasions upon which this bill was before us, I should like to state now that I support a bill of rights for Canada. We live in a country which has a wide expanse; we have people of many races, many creeds and different customs. Because of these differences I think we need something to bind us together so that we will become a nation. I recognize the fact that many of the freedoms and fundamental rights that are mentioned in this bill are already on the statute books of Canada. However, I feel it is a good thing to bring them to our notice, and I think it is a good thing to bring them to our notice in the terms of a bill of rights. I think they will mean something to all Canadians, particularly to new Canadians.
I, too, Mr. Chairman, in some respects am a new Canadian. I say to the committee now that I am a new Canadian and I am proud of it. I believe there are thousands of my countrymen who are proud of this, too. I say, as well, that if their loyalty to this nation is ever excelled it will only be by the loyalty of those who have always had the privilege of calling themselves Canadians.
Again, I say we live in a country that has a wide expanse and in which there are many differences. The bill of rights will serve once again to unite us into one nation. Unity without freedom could very well be tyranny. Multiplicity, on the other hand, might very well be chaos. I think one of the great strengths of the Canadian nation is that we have a unity in multiplicity. Perhaps it is in building up that unity in multiplicity that our bill of rights becomes very important, for no nation can be cemented together until its people as individuals recognize that freedom is not licence to do what we want to do, but the privilege of doing what we ought to do.
I would have liked to see a national bill of rights. I can see the difficulties in the way. I would have liked to see a stronger bill of rights than we have now. Again I can see some difficulties in the way there. But not having either of these, Mr. Chairman, I am going to support the bill of rights as we have it today.
The work in the committee was rather concentrated. We had a comparatively large number of witnesses over a comparatively short space of time. I think the bill now before us, which has just come out of the special committee, is better than the bill which went into the committee. I am not going to recount any further the work of this committee; that has been done by other members of the committee and I am sure will be well known to those who have read the evidence.
IMr. Batten.]
But I do think that we did not have quite enough time to do the important job that was entrusted to us. I think maybe if we had had more time and this bill had been brought into the house earlier in the session, there would have been the possibility of having before the committee more witnesses with a greater diversity of opinion. I also think many Canadians with strong feelings about the bill of rights would have made presentations if there had been more time for them to do so. Certainly for many of those who would have liked to come to this committee, they had little time to prepare the evidence which they would have liked to submit.
Then again, another thing which I thought was important was that some of the briefs which were presented, either written or in oral form, were worthy of more study, and when the committee was operating at the pace it was there was little time to give the presentations the type of attention they deserved.
I do not quite agree with the hon. member for Charlotte. He and I sat on this committee together and I appreciate the opportunity I had of knowing and appreciating him better, both as a member of parliament and as a man. But both of us having sat on the bill of rights I know he is going to accord me the right of differing with him. I do not think there was enough time to give this bill the attention which it deserved, and I do not think the Canadian Labour Congress took the view he suggested it did. Mr. Chairman, let me read from page 2 of their brief, as set out on page 191 of volume 3 of the evidence. The Canadian Labour Congress said this:
First and foremost, it feels that at this stage of a session of parliament the present bill cannot receive from this committee the careful and thorough consideration it ought to receive.
The brief went on further to say:
Great issues, profound issues, issues of immense legal difficulty, are at stake. It is simply impossible for any individual, however learned, however eloquent, however long he has considered these questions, to present his views adequately upon a few days' notice. It is simply impossible for all the individuals who should be heard to make their views known to you within the compass of five or six days. And what is true of individuals is even truer of organizations, which, in the nature of things, need more time to prepare their submissions.
This is not the way to deal with questions of such import. It is not seemly. It does not give the people of Canada the chance they ought to have, and were led to expect they would have, to present their views with that coherence and order which so high a matter demands.
I think there were others, too, who made presentations before this committee who regretted the fact that this bill had not been brought in earlier and been given more time

for the study of its various implications. We did have individuals who came and gave their private opinions. We also had individuals who presented briefs on behalf of organizations. I was one of those who thought some representatives from the provinces should have presented briefs on behalf of the provinces. I am not referring now to the constitutional rights of the provinces or the question of the constitutionality of the bill; I am referring to the fact that if we had one representative before the committee representing a certain organization, surely some representative from each of the ten provinces should also have had the right to appear before this committee.
I further believe that additional progress could have been made toward a national bill if earlier in the year an effort had been made to contact the provinces and ascertain their feelings on this very important matter. In fact, from statements made at the recent federal-provincial conference there were indications that perhaps we could get a little nearer to agreement on this matter than we thought possible a month ago. However, I think we as Canadians can look forward to the time when other steps will be taken in this very important period of constitutional history in our country, and that in time a national bill of rights will become a reality for all Canadians.

Mr. Chairman, I would like at the outset to express, as did the hon. member for Fort William, the intense pride and honour that I felt was mine to sit on this committee on the bill of rights. I subscribe to everything he said with the exception of the very kind, and I must say gratuitous, reference that he made to me as chairman of that committee.
It is true that at the outset we on the committee did run into troubled waters and rough weather, and if it had not been for the fact that we had a very excellent crew I am afraid we might have lost our cargo. However, the storm subsided just about as quickly as it arose, and from that point on we enjoyed the work he had to do together, and in due course of time we completed our work, brought our ship into port and landed our cargo. It is true that in the process of reaching port we did take on a little additional cargo, but I must say that the bill of rights which we reported to this house is essentially and fundamentally the same bill of rights which was assigned to us for study.
I was rather surprised when the hon. member for Assiniboia expressed the opinion that this bill as reported contained about 50 per cent of new material. I must differ with that. I think a study of the bill which is before 79951-0-468J
Human Rights
us now, apart from the preamble which it was indicated at the outset would be an acceptable addition, would show there have been only five changes made in this measure. First of all in clause 1, which is the clause now before the committee, there was a change made which emphasized rather than added the right to the freedoms which are set forth in that clause, without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex. Those words were simply taken out of subclause (b) of that clause and were added to the premises for the purpose, as I think, of emphasizing that these rights and freedoms were to be enjoyed by everyone without discrimination.
In that respect I think we set at rest what may be referred to by some as criticisms. I do not look upon them as being that. I look upon them as being only constructive suggestions.
We made three additions to clause 2, and again I emphasize that these are not matters which were not included in the general enumeration of rights and freedoms in clause 1. Clause 2, after all, is the interpretative clause, and it is in that clause that an attempt is made to spell out in particular those things to which the courts must have regard when it comes to the interpretation or the application of the laws of the parliament of Canada.
These changes involved, first of all, the removal from subclause (b) of the words that were contained therein as to the imposition of torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. What the committee did in this instance was to substitute for those words the phrase "cruel and unusual treatment or punishment". I am not going to deal with reasons for that, as these will come up later when we come to consider this particular clause, but fundamentally it was the same language we had in that clause before, except that we wanted to make it clear that it did not contemplate the abrogation of any punishment in the present Criminal Code.
The other two changes in this clause were made in subclause (f), and again I say that this was only for the purpose of spelling out in greater detail, without becoming too verbose, those rights and freedoms declared in the first clause of the bill. What was added, then, v/as a well known and well recognized basic principle of criminal law in this country, namely that a person shall be presumed innocent until proved guilty; and along with that we added at the end of that clause the rights to reasonable bail unless there was just cause for refusing it. These are rights which are already preserved in our Criminal Code, but because of the suggestions made

Human Rights
by many that we should proceed a little further in clause 2 to spell out in detail the rights and freedoms stated, the committee went along with the suggestions to add those provisions.
The fifth and last change has to do with the next clause, which relates to the functions of the Minister of Justice. There was a good deal of consideration given to the matter. He had to examine the statutes and it was uncertain, having done that, what his duties should be. Now the clause sets forth his duties, and so on. It was considered desirable to add to that clause the words to be found at the end of the present clause 3, namely that at the first opportunity he should report to the house any inconsistency relating to acts of parliament or regulations passed or intended to be passed.
That is the sum and substance of the changes which have been made in this bill. The other things we did were simply to rearrange the contents and make it perhaps a better bill, in that the bill of rights would be in a form suitable for posting on the walls of schools, church assembly halls and so on, and perhaps make it a little more readily understandable by the layman.
Now, having indicated that the bill which we have reported is essentially the same bill we received, I should like to add my voice to the many others who have spoken for this bill not only during the four days of debate on second reading but previously in this committee. The Prime Minister, as we know, has for years advocated a bill of rights in written form. He has devoted a great deal of his time in this house to urging upon the government of the day that this should be done. No one, I believe, has worked any harder to bring about a removal of the prejudices that unfortunately still exist in this country, and to bring about unity not only between the two great races in this land, the French and the English, but also between those of other races or their descendants who have come and joined us in establishing a Canadian nation.
At this stage I should like to put on record a matter that was referred to by the Prime Minister when he spoke on July 1. That was the resolution the hon. gentleman introduced in the House of Commons on May 3, 1946, at the time the house was considering amendments to the Citizenship Act. I do so in order to indicate that as far back as 14 years ago the Prime Minister held the views that he holds today and which in the main are embodied in the bill before us. The motion moved by the hon. gentleman on that occasion was in these words:

That the following words be added to the section as subsection 6: "Such certificate of citizenship shall be deemed to include a bill of rights as follows:
1.	Freedom of religion, freedom of speech, and the right to peaceable assembly are assured.
2.	Habeas corpus shall not be suspended except by parliament.
3.	No one shall be required to give evidence before any tribunal or commission at any time if denied counsel or other constitutional safeguards."
That was the resolution introduced at that time. From that time forward, year in and year out, the records of parliament will show that the Prime Minister has persisted in advocating the early adoption of a bill of rights in statutory form.
Before referring to some of the views expressed by those who appeared before the committee perhaps I may be allowed to put on record the names of the organizations and individuals who appeared, in view of the references made by the last hon. member who spoke. It is true that the committee dealt with this bill in a reasonably short period of time, but the committee worked diligently and thoroughly. In that period of time the committee held no less than 25 meetings and heard representations from the following: Professor F. R. Scott of McGill University; Professor C. P. Wright of Ottawa University; Professor C. R. Dehler of St. Eustache sur le Lac; Rev. D. L. Michael, executive secretary of the Seventh Day Adventist church in Canada; Mr. Saul Hayes, Q.C., executive secretary of the Canadian Jewish congress; Mr. Donald Mclnnes, Q.C., dominion vice president of the Canadian Bar Association and representing that association; Professor Bowker, dean of the faculty of law of the University of Alberta; Mr. Irving Himel, Q.C., executive secretary of the association for civil liberties; Mr. Claude Jodoin, president, as well as other officials, representing the Canadian Labour Congress; Mr. F. R. Varcoe, Q.C., a former deputy attorney general for Canada; Mr. L. A. Tufts, representing the Christian Science committee on publications of the Christian Science church; Professor A. R. Lower of Queen's University; Professor O. E. Lang of the faculty of law of the University of Saskatchewan; Professor Maxwell Cohen, acting dean of the faculty of law of McGill University and Mr. D. W. Mundell, Q.C., who for two years was chairman of the civil liberties section of the Canadian Bar Association.
That is a formidable list of witnesses who appeared before the committee. In addition we had the Minister of Justice with us at several meetings explaining and dealing with the various clauses of the bill. The committee also had before it briefs which were submitted in written form. Other persons and

organizations had also been contacted but did not appear before the committee, because in most instances it was indicated to the committee that their points of view had already been presented to it.
I suppose that a committee sitting to discuss a bill as important and far-reaching as this could go on endlessly hearing witnesses. Every time publicity was given to the views of a witness before the committee we would at once receive word that somebody holding a different view would like to appear. I am convinced in my own mind, as I am sure every hon. member of the committee is, that we had placed before us every conceivable point of view which could be advanced in regard to this bill, and that no useful purpose would have been served by having two, three, four or more witnesses appearing before the committee to present essentially the same argument.
I think that also applies to this committee. In that respect I hope to avoid repeating the arguments advanced by other hon. members of the committee. Reiteration of the same point of view is not what was needed by the committee that dealt with the bill. I am confident that we had before us all the points of view that could be presented, and that no useful purpose would have been served by continuing to hear further points of view or having the committee sit at greater length.
May I refer to the views expressed by Rev. D. L. Michael on behalf of the Seventh Day Adventist church in Canada, which appear on page 70 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence. He said this:
The Prime Minister and government are to be commended for the genuine concern in the preservation and extension of human rights that the introduction of this bill represents. Members of the Adventist Church in Canada have watched with great interest the efforts of the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, Hon. David A. Croll, Mr. M. J. Coldwell, Hon. Arthur W. Roebuck and many others to secure the basic rights of Canadian citizens through a comprehensive bill of rights.
The work of many public spirited individuals now finds fruition in this step that the parliament of Canada is being asked to take. The passage of this measure will mark an historic and significant milestone for this country in its quest for freedom and peace under the rule of law.
I am not going to repeat them, but the hon. member for Greenwood earlier in this debate referred to the words of Professor Lower somewhat along the same line. Again, may I read from page 132 of the evidence the opinion expressed by Mr. Hayes on behalf of the Canadian Jewish Congress. He said:
We highly commend the Canadian government for having introduced Bill C-79 and recommend its early adoption with such refinements of text as the labours of this committee will produce.
There were others who appeared before the committee and expressed similar views. It
Human Rights
is true there were some who felt that a bill of rights such as this should be somehow enshrined in the constitution, but I think without exception-there may have been some mental reservations-everyone admitted that in any event this was a first step and a big step toward that ultimate which some of them thought desirable.
Much has been said about the views of Professor Scott. As has been said, the professor did not have very many fine things to say about this bill, but he did have a view to express which I think I should refer to because to my mind it was a retrograde step that he felt the committee and parliament should take. In that connection may I read what he said at page 24 of the evidence.
A method by which an amendment could be obtained without necessarily having prior consultations with the provinces is; if the parliament of Canada wished, it could secure a constitutional amendment which would take away from itself in the future the power to make Canadian statutes contrary to certain basic human rights. It could do that-and since the amendment would in no way affect the present rights of the provinces, the prior agreement of the provinces to that constitutional change would, in my opinion, not be necessary-no consultation would be necessary. If the parliament of Canada wishes to have less legislative authority than it now possesses, there is nothing to prevent it, as it were giving that authority back to the United Kingdom parliament and leaving it there for the time being.
If I understood the professor, that simply meant that to enshrine those rights and freedoms in a constitution so it could not be changed by this or a subsequent parliament, he had in mind the retrograde step of returning to the United Kingdom the powers which over the years we have consistently advocated should be removed from the United Kingdom and brought to Canada. Therefore it appears to me that in the view of some who criticized this bill on the ground that they would prefer to have a constitutional amendment, in order to have the kind of amendment which would not be subject to change we would have to surrender some of our Canadian sovereignty.
What has been Canadian history, particularly over recent years? It has obviously been an attempt by the people to obtain rights against the state. First of all, as we go back into English history-and I must say that in his evidence Professor Cohen gave us a very good but rather lengthy review of the evolution of the freedoms that we enjoy today-we find that the power of the crown was supreme. Then there was a contest to remove that power from the sovereign and give it to parliament. In time that did succeed, but there was also at the same time a contest between the power of the state and the individual and that went on-
