Mr. Chairman, I thank the committee for extending this privilege to me, and I will make my remaining remarks as brief as I possibly can. May I at this point refer to a matter mentioned by the Prime Minister during the course of his remarks in the debate on the bill; namely the Quebec Act, passed in 1774 which, as hon. members will recall, granted freedom of religion to the people of the province of Quebec, which at that time comprised practically all of Canada as it was then constituted. With that, of course, went the freedom to profess and practise the religion of the church of Rome. This measure preceded the granting of freedom of religion in the United Kingdom.
Hon. members will also recall that at that time slavery existed in the provinces of Canada. Immediately after the passing of the act which divided the then province of Quebec into Upper and Lower Canada we find that in 1793 an act was passed in Upper Canada for the abolition of slavery. This act passed in our country preceded by 40 years the statute of the United Kingdom of 1833 which abolished slavery throughout all British possessions. I think it is desirable to quote from the act of 1793, which provided in part as follows:
No negro or other person who shall come or be brought into this province. .. shall be subject to the condition of a slave or to bounden involuntary service for life.
Of course that did not free slaves already in Upper Canada, but the act went on to provide that every child born after the passing of the act of a negro mother or other woman subjected to such service should become absolutely free on attaining the age of 25, the master in the meantime to provide proper nourishment and clothing for the child. The act further declared that all issue of such children would be free whenever born.
Here in Upper Canada, a British colony abolished slavery by legislation for the first time. The struggle for the emancipation of man as against the power of the state and as against other individuals went on. True, in the course of time we came to feel, mainly through the courts, that there existed a natural law under which we had certain well

defined rights and freedoms, but they were never embodied in a statute; and it was undoubtedly the view of the Prime Minister that at the very first opportunity that would avail itself to him he should urge that this be done. It must afford great satisfaction to him that now, after many years of struggle and effort, parliament has before it and I hope will enact, a statute which will be a monument to him, and something of which not only the Prime Minister but all of us who have participated in the work of the special committee and in the consideration of the measure in parliament will be justly proud in years to come.

Mr. Chairman, I have no great contribution to make to this debate, but I do want to frame a few questions for the Minister of Justice as one particularly interested in this legislation. I wish to refer him to an introduction that he wrote several years ago to a book called "Freedom Wears a Crown", by John Farthing. To be more explicit, I am very much interested that he should have a part-I assume he has a part and is in essence helping to sponsor the bill -in something that gives no recognition to the great theme of this book of which he approved in such forthright terms in the introduction. If I read several paragraphs I think I will make my point. I assume that the E. D. Fulton mentioned here is the minister, and in the introduction on page 16 I find this paragraph:
The second thesis is that in Canada we chose, as our political system, the crown in parliament, with its ideal of individual liberty guaranteed by the written and unwritten laws governing the relationship of the three constituent elements, crown, cabinet and commons. The choice of that constitutional system was a free and deliberate decision made by Canadians and accepted equally by the two main elements of the population of Canada.
The minister, before he was a minister, went on to approve to a great extent of the general theme presented by Mr. Farthing, and I wish to read several paragraphs from the book. I should like the minister's comment thereon in relation to the measure now before us. On page 142 there is the following:
Our constitutional inheritance was the living product of a long process of historical growth and development, and the tradition it embodied is of an order already proven of value in dealing vith changing conditions of life and with changing climates of opinion. Such an order and such a tradition are not things that must of necessity be cast aside because the world has changed since the days of Queen Victoria. The British constitution was not the product of the Victorian age, and the British tradition is in no way bound to or fettered by any historical epoch. Indeed that is the essential point of contrast as it is also the essential glory of the British tradition as compared with the American. Their constitution binds the Americans to the ideas and mental climate of the

eighteenth century. They are tied, as it were, and for all time, to the apron strings of George Washington.
We are not so tied. On the contrary, we inherit an ever-living historical tradition; ever-living precisely because it is historical; because in every successive age it has been drawing sustaining life from established roots and giving new strength to that life by drawing new food from new sources. It has been and remains a truly creative power, not carried about by every wind that blows, but meeting the present always in the firm assurance of the past with the resources of wisdom and of strength that can only be found in such an assurance, and in such a source.
Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister on various occasions, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs the other day, indicated in reply to questions by the hon. member for Assiniboia the deep interest and devotion of the members of the government to the British tradition and the crown, and the great respect they have for the mother of parliaments. I am not arguing that there should have been included in this bill any reference to the crown and the British tradition, but I do think we deserve an explanation from the minister or someone on the government side as to their reason for not including some reference to what I think is the most important part of our tradition. The minister was so forthright in his reference to the crown in parliament and the constitution as something that is above and beyond the government, the emphasis being upon the system rather than upon the members of the government-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would the hon. member like an answer to that now? I can give it to him in a few words.

I shall complete my remarks very shortly. I have looked through the bill as amended, and I can see no touchstone-and I thought we might find one-in the preamble to the British parliamentary tradition. I am speaking personally, and not in a party sense. One of my great regrets is that we teach so little British history in this country, which could be a part of our tradition.
I should like some explanation from the government as to why this measure, which the government regards as of such fundamental importance, does not contain at least some recognition of that particular part of our tradition. I know it was argued, as I remember, by Mr. Garson, the minister of justice in the previous administration, that one of the reasons we did not need a bill of rights in this country was that we were within this mainstream of the British tradition, so it had not been found necessary to enunciate it. Obviously this government does not believe that Mr. Garson had the right approach.
However, the view is widely held by many people in Canada, I would not say the
Human Rights
majority, that one of the great guarantees of our liberties is the crown in parliament and the British tradition. I should like an explanation as to why this does not seem to have found recognition in this particular document. Wherever we turn in Canadian life we find references to such things as the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation. The minister said he was proud to get up and speak as a representative in parliament of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The Prime Minister is creating such things as royal commissions. A great deal of our language, in so far as parliamentary terms in concerned, and a great many of our procedures go back to this tradition, and I am wondering if those words are going to become completely meaningless unless they find some recognition in this bill.
I realize that I have perhaps given too much detail and obscured my point, but I am asking from an individual rather than from a party point of view as to why there was not a recognition within this document itself of that particular point of view, especially in the light of what I have always taken to be a part of the tradition of the Progressive Conservative party.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think this point deserves an answer at once, Mr. Chairman. I should like to say to the hon. gentleman that there is, in my view, no inconsistency between this bill and the views I expressed in the foreword of the book to which he was kind enough to refer or the views expressed in the book itself by the late Mr. Farthing. Explicit in those passages was the view that the Canadian tradition, coming down from the British tradition in this field, is a parliamentary tradition. Parliament means the crown in parliament, our parliament depending for its life, its living force, upon the necessary presence of three elements, including the crown. Well, that most certainly is embodied in this statute. It is embodied in the phrase, "Therefore Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows".
I suggest this seriously to my hon. friend. I am not trying to minimize his point by referring to this as a small thing, it is a very important tradition, and this expression which appears in every Canadian statute embodies that tradition. It is correct to speak about the crown in parliament for it is the crown, by and with the consent of the Senate and the House of Commons, that enacts the statutes under which the Canadian people live. That is parliament. You will observe that we have started the preamble in this way:
The parliament of Canada, affirming that the Canadian nation is founded upon principles that acknowledge-

Human Rights
Affirming also that men and institutions remain free-
And being desirous of enshrining these principles-
-in a statute, and then we say-
Therefore Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
That is parliament acting, and it is the crown in parliament, so it is complete. It flows from that very tradition and recognizes the living authority of the tradition which was discussed in that book.

I acknowledge this, and I noted that particular part in the preamble. However, this part is in the preamble of every statute we enact. It is the argument of the government that this bill is of fundamental importance. We have this preamble in response to what I and many other members requested, something that would be a ringing declaration which could be used in the schools. While I can agree that this preamble is much more worth-while than what we had before, still there is no reference within the preamble either to the crown or to the British tradition. I just wondered why it was not thought proper to put it in.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think I can give the answer. The bill of rights is not concerned with a definition of the elements of the constitution, of the elements of parliament itself. It is concerned with a declaration of the rights of the people of Canada. It is because the constitutional tradition is a tradition within this parliament which enacts the bill that it is not necessary to define that tradition in terms of saying what is the constitution defining the elements of the parliament that is enacting this bill. We know that because that is part of our tradition. If at any time we have to look it up we go to the British North America Act which is, in itself, the basic document of the Canadian constitution. We find there a definition of our constitution. We find there the passage I had in mind in that portion of the foreword to which reference was made, namely:
Whereas the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick have expressed their desire to be federally united into one dominion under the crown of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, with a constitution similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom:
We find, therefore, within the British North America Act itself an outline of what constitutes our parliament, the House of Commons and the Senate, and it is a parliament with the crown; that is our constitution and that is our parliament. It did not seem to us

proper or necessary to define our constitution in a bill of rights, which is a bill enacted by parliament and concerned with a declaration of the rights of individuals in Canada.

Would the minister agree that this clause affirms that the Canadian nation is founded upon principles, and then the preamble goes on; and would the minister not agree that those principles are, in the main, inherent in the British parliamentary traditions?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I think that is true, too, but their traditions recognize these principles. But here the land of principles we are talking about are principles that primarily relate to and give foundation for and validity to the rights and liberties of the individual. We are concerned with a bill of rights here rather than a definition of constitutional principles.

Mr. Chairman, as a member of this committee I wish to make a few general remarks. I would, however, like to say to the Minister of Justice who has been active in the prosecution of this measure that when we come to the various clauses I am sure he will expect a more detailed discussion than is possible at this juncture.
I would like to join with my colleagues on the committee in expressing a word of thanks to the chairman, my fellow townsman, for his direction of our work, and to all members of the committee regardless of their political interest for the serious and responsible attention that they gave to the deliberations of the committee, which came unfortunately toward the end of the session, and involved 25 meetings in little less than three weeks, thereby imposing on all of the members of that committee a task which was by no means easy to accept.
I believe we now have before the house a bill in an improved form, a bill that has undergone substantial modification, considerable tightening up and, generally speaking, within the limits available to us, a much more effective document.
During the course of the committee's proceedings the Minister of Justice paid a tribute to Mr. Driedger who, he said, had formulated most of the terms of the bill before us, when we were on second reading. I think it is only right, when tributes are being paid, to acknowledge the author of the bill that was before the house on second reading.
We had before us during the 25 sittings of our committee some distinguished jurists, historians and constitutional authorities. We

in the Liberal party, who as the hon. member for Charlotte so generously said took our responsibilities seriously, were I think able to suggest most of the individual people, apart from organizations, who came before the committee. We are grateful and indebted, therefore, to Professors Scott, Bowker, Cohen, Lang, Lower and Wright, and Mr. David Mundell.
I regret very much that Mr. Carter, who had strong views about the concept of a bill of rights itself, was not able to participate in our discussions, although he wrote a letter available for all to read. I regret, too that Professor Bora Laskin, who must be recognized as one of the foremost authorities on constitutional law and practice in our country, was not available; and I regret of course that Mr. Louis-Philippe Pigeon of Laval University who communicated vicariously with the hon. member for Bellechasse did not appear before the committee because his views with regard to those parts of the bill that touch on provincial powers were very important in our considerations. They had much to do with the acknowledged limitation of the federal government in this field, and as now stated in the preamble of the bill.
We did our best to propose further modifications to the bill, which were not recognized by the majority of the members of the committee or by the Minister of Justice. I believe that time will show those amendments which were not accepted would have considerably improved the scope of the bill and would have been in keeping with the evolutionary character of the conception of rights which, in a growing society, from one period to another, will become more and more apparent as time goes on. Thus we have learned in the twentieth century that rights and duties, while they may continue to be in some measure the same, nevertheless have expanded through new concepts which have given rise to new rights and corresponding duties.
The Leader of the Opposition last night mentioned that we now have in the bill a preamble. He observed that when the suggestion was first made on second reading it was ridiculed by the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that is not correct. What I was talking about was poetic language. No specific objection was taken to a preamble.

I would regard the characterization of a preamble as poetic language to be the kind of ridicule one would expect from a man whose brilliance we must recognize in the person of the Minister of Justice. Brilliant men have their method of
Human Rights
deriding something that is good. I regard this particular form of derision, cynicism or satire as a criticism of the suggestion for a preamble.
In any event we now have a preamble, and I must say that we are grateful to the minister and his officers who acted as a sort of co-ordinator for the various suggestions of preambles which were made by different members of the committee, among them the hon. member for Fort William, the hon. member for Bellechasse, the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort, and several other hon. members. I had the honour of proposing one myself. But I believe that the preamble now in the bill, not fully satisfactory as we shall indicate when we get into the more detailed discussion stage, is perhaps one of the satisfactory features of the bill in that it does enable a greater appreciation of the implications of this bill of rights, short as it is of being a national bill and not completely satisfactory in terms of the effect which flows from the attempt to give it the power of a legal enactment.
Nevertheless the preamble is something which I believe deserves emphasis, because it incorporates three concepts which were not fully present, or in two particulars, not present at all, in the bill as originally presented.
First of all, there is stated in the bill that the Canadian nation is founded on principles which acknowledge the supremacy of God. I am happy to say as a member of the committee that every member readily supported the idea that in a document of this kind in Canada there should be an acknowledgment of the religious character of this country and of the recognition that Canadians, generally speaking, accord to God himself.
I thought that the observations of the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort in stating his views in this particular were impressive and will for a long time remain with me. He said, as I indeed had previously indicated in the committee, that we were divided between two main ideologies so-called, the one based on dialectical materialism, and recognition or belief in the supremacy of man, the other based on spiritual and moral values, which take their form in a belief in the supremacy of God. In a document of this kind there should be no hesitation on the part of nations like our own in affirming this fact. I believe it is well that we should have taken this decision. I think it is a decision which was taken, not with any political consideration in mind but as one subscribed to by all those members present on the committee representing all the political parties.

Human Rights
Then there is the recognition of a suggestion which was made by this particular party, that there should be reposed in the preamble an acknowledgment that the Canadian family is an essential constituent of our society. I must say in all fairness to the hon. member for Bellechasse, that he had distributed a preamble, which had not been put forward officially but in which he did recognize the importance of the Canadian family as the basis of a society of free men and institutions.
Because many of us on the committee and because many of the constitutional experts outside were concerned about the fact that clause 2 of the bill did seem to touch provincial powers, or at any rate was so worded as to create doubt in the minds of those who were disposed to examine the proposition, we did suggest that either in the preamble or in some other clause in the bill words should be included which would clearly establish that this bill was not intended to touch upon, and that it did not in fact touch upon, any powers which did not come within section 91 of the British North America Act or which did not come within the powers of the federal parliament. I am not fully satisfied, as I have privately indicated to the Minister of Justice, that in the English version of the text we have completely made this clear, but I am satisfied that in the French text we have succeeded in doing so. The French text at this point reads:
(Translation):
-which shall reflect the respect of parliament for the provisions of its constitutional authority.
(Text):
It seems to me that when we come to examine the preamble, we shall have to use words of strength in order to meet the point of view we have in mind. There have been suggestions we should use the words "within its legislative competence" and that certainly would have been satisfactory to me.
May I, even at the expense of being accused of false pride, join with my colleague the hon. member for Fort William and put on the record of this house my own thought as to what should have been in the preamble by reading the very words that I proposed. These were:
Before God, the Canadian people, united for the common pursuit of their well-being, composed of persons of various races and religions from many nations; intent on preserving the dignity of the individual in his rights and freedoms, which have been secured through the institution of parliament and the law, desire to reaffirm their faith in these human rights and fundamental freedoms.
Having joined with other nations and their peoples in the universal declaration of human rights, the people of Canada rededicate themselves to the principles of that charter in its human,

social, political, economic and legal terms, particularly those concerning the sanctity and inviolability of the family as the fundamental unit of society, the right of the individual to participate in government and to earn a living for himself and his family.
The Canadian people, therefore, believe that it is meet and proper that, for the better understanding of all, the parliament of Canada declare before man and God, on behalf of the nation, those human rights, fundamental freedoms, and objects of national purpose that are within its competence so to do.
In any event, I was among those whose text was not fully accepted, but it will be recognized, as in the case of most other suggestions, that the composite arrangement put forward by the Minister of Justice through the efforts of the law offices officers does meet the chief objectives we had in mind.
I simply want to say it would possibly be a waste of time to try to add up the suggestions which were made by this party or by that, but it is significant that the members of this party, like the members of the Conservative party, did in their individual capacities make valuable suggestions. I can hardly agree with the member of the committee, who has just spoken that the extent of our contribution was to be measured merely by five different acceptances. When we get into more detailed discussion, I think it will be possible to show that the extent of the contribution made by those in this party was much greater and amounted to more numerically than the hon. member seemed to accept.
It is significant that in clause 2(f) of the bill before us the amendment dealing with the legal right of the presumption of innocence and the matter of granting reasonable bail to an accused were accepted in principle by the committee, and are now incorporated in the bill. The anti-discrimination clause has been strengthened as a result of suggestions put forward as an amendment by members of this party. I mention this not because I wish to discriminate against members of the Conservative party-that is not my intention -but to indicate that the contribution of the members of this party was, as the hon. member for Charlotte so generously pointed out, a valuable one.
We are particularly reminded of the contribution made by the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway, who I think more than any other member was responsible for extricating the minister from what I would call at least an intellectual dilemma, if not a dilemma of another kind, because of the words "torture, cruel and degrading punishment" which he had in the old clause 2(b). So there were contributions made by many hon. members, which have resulted in a considerable improvement in this document.

I listened with great interest to what the hon. member for Bellechasse had to say in his able speech earlier today.
(Translation):
The hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion) related the question of provincial civil rights with that of family rights. There is not the slightest doubt that, if this bill were to encroach upon family rights within the province, it would be ultra vires, or beyond the jurisdiction of the federal government.
However the member for Bellechasse himself recognized, and still admits today, that the effect of the bill is limited' to the legislative jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada.
Therefore, it is only within the legislative jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada that we want to affirm the rights and the protection of the rights of the Canadian family.
The member for Bellechasse has always voted in favour of the social security measures which constitute the correlative rights of the Canadian family.
We want those rights protected by the bill of rights. May I point out too that his previous leaders were not always in favour of those measures, for instance, the one respecting family allowances.
We are thinking of the future, and we want to make those family rights as inviolable as possible.
The stand taken by the Quebec premier during the federal provincial conference was not inconsistent with that taken by his party in the Quebec legislature on February 3, 1960.
It will be remembered that in February, 1960, the Quebec legislature took a look at the bill of rights, which was given its first reading on June 27. Now in that bill there was no reference to the legislative limitation of the parliament of Canada.
On July 1, the Prime Minister clearly indicated in his statement that the scope of this bill was limited to the legislative jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. Later on, we succeeded in having a preamble added which clearly sets forth the legislative limits beyond which the Canadian parliament may not go.
Under the circumstances the doubts expressed by the Quebec legislature as to constitutionality were justified. The preamble, however, does away with any constitutional uncertainties.
I think that the member for Bellechasse accepts my interpretation of the subject he has dealt with.
(Text):
While this bill is not all that we would like it to be and while I should like to see
Human Rights
a national bill and one entrenched in the constitution, nevertheless there was never any suggestion by anyone in this party or for that matter in the committee that this bill should be delayed at this time. The only suggestion-and that was in the form of a motion-was that while the federal-provincial fiscal conference was under way, we might wait until the deliberations of the conferees had been settled before proceeding. That would not have taken us beyond the Friday of the week in which the conference took place.
I feel that a bill of rights that is not part of the constitution is not satisfactory. To the extent that this bill goes, it is welcome, but it must be recognized that in its present form in law it will be subject to the rule of interpretation, which I think we will all recognize, and that general statements-and that is what we have in this bill at the present time-must give way to existing specific statutes whether or not they are inconsistent with this bill.
Because I believe that the present bill, consisting as it does of a valuable declaration, adds nothing to our fundamental law-it does not alter it, but generally speaking, it does not add anything to our fundamental law-and because of its general terms it could not be regarded as having legal effect in itself, I believe-and this is the substance of most of the evidence before the committee-of amending any existing statutes which might be regarded as inconsistent with this bill of rights.
I am sure that this general declaration, valuable as it is, will go no further than the courts have already gone in their decisions. What are required in this bill, it seems to me, and what I hope we will consider at some stage of our deliberations, are ways and means of clearly establishing by enactment that all bills inconsistent with this measure are in fact repealed hereby.
I have on the order paper a bill the purpose of which is to amend the Expropriation Act. I hope that we can deal with this bill before we rise and prorogue, because as long as that measure is on the statute books in its present form and as long as its provisions continue to be the law, there will be involved, as the very reading of this proposed amendment indicates, a violation of human rights not by one individual against another but by the crown against the Canadian citizen.
There are other acts which are inconsistent with this bill. They will continue to be the law of the land unless this bill is so modified as to make clear the intention of parliament, that notwithstanding what

Human Rights
they may now contain all such acts are to the extent of their inconsistency abrogated by this measure.
We cannot say we are fully satisfied with the bill in all of its particulars, subject to the amending modifications that I have indicated we will deal with later. There is, of course, the point made by the Leader of the Opposition, that is that the War Measures Act needs a liberalization that may take it to a closer relationship to the guarantees provided for by way of declaration in this bill of rights. It is no answer to say this is not a matter we can discuss, because the government itself in this very measure has already provided for a repeal of some of its provisions. It is no answer to say we will look at this question as a whole in another session. Now is the time when all these matters are incorporated in the same document for us to deal with them so as to reduce to the lowest possible minimum those violations of human rights and fundamental freedoms which we seek to protect in this bill.
There is a whole range of other rights that must be recognized in the kind of society we have at the present time, a society different from that of our fathers and different from that of the liberal-minded men who acted as precursors of the liberal emancipations in earlier centuries. We have an opportunity now, which we must seize while this bill is being discussed in this chamber to give effect to these new concepts and new obligations, referred to by implication in some respects in the preamble of the bill.
This bill is acceptable. It is welcome to the extent that it goes. We are happy to have contributed to an improvement in the quality and in the form of this bill. I think that all hon. members who served on the committee regardless of party and notwithstanding what may have been the misinterpretations of motive and purpose in the early days of our sitting would agree that we, delegated by this house, fulfilled our responsibility as well as we knew how. We have produced a document which, because of limitations not capable of correction by us, is not all that we would like it to be but nevertheless is now in a much more presentable form than it was when it left this chamber after second reading.
I conclude with this. It seems to me this bill will rely for its strength, not on the letter of the law, which is sought to be expressed, not in the decisions of our courts, which will ultimately be given,-and there will be much judicial law making because of the uncertainties and ambiguities, because of the doubtful powers, here and there, which have been pointed out by the hon. member for Charlotte-the raison d'etre of this bill will be found largely in the disposition and

in the attitude that Canadians take one toward another. Through tolerance and generous appreciation of the rights of one's neighbour, we in this Canadian nation will be able to see grow and strengthen the advantages of liberty and freedom.
I should like to conclude what I have to say by saying the tolerance and the unity that we look for in Canada which is basic in this bill was expressed by Sir Wilfrid Laurier more eloquently than anyone that I know when, speaking to a group of students during the days when he was one of the great statesmen of our country, he said this:
Three years ago, when in England, X visited one of those models of Gothic architecture, which the hand of genius, guided by an unerring faith had moulded into an harmonious whole. That cathedral is made of marble, oak and granite. It is the image of the nation I would like to see Canada become. Here, I want the marble to remain the marble; the oak, the oak; the granite, the granite. Out of these elements, I would build a nation great among the nations of the world.

Mr. Chairman, I shall not traverse the ground which I covered on previous occasions; indeed, my remarks today will be limited by the fact that on many previous occasions I have dealt at length with this matter. I would be less than frank, Mr. Chairman, if I were not to say to you how much I feel the discussions that have taken place in the last 14 years as to the need of a bill of rights in Canada have borne fruit. This is evidenced by the views now expressed by the hon. member for Essex East who, with commendable eloquence, paid his tribute to the need of a bill of rights in Canada although still continuing to hold the view expressed by others in the opposition and elsewhere that before a bill of rights can become finally effective in a national sense a constitutional amendment will be required.
I intend to take but a few moments to refer to the great transition that has taken place, for all during those years from 1946 to 1957 there was never at any time any support from those who then occupied the treasury benches of this country, although in the Liberal party support did come from two hon. members, both of whom are today in the Senate of Canada, namely Senator Roebuck and Senator Croll, as well as from Alistair Stewart, a former member of this house, and Mr. M. J. Coldwell, the leader of the C.C.F. party. I say this not by way of criticism, but it indicates how in the passage of time reformation does take place. From the attitude of the treasury benches of this country in the days of 1946 to 1957 we have now passed to the position where hon. gentlemen such as the hon. member for Essex East now give to a bill of rights support which in past years they did not accord to it.

In this connection, I think I might read the words of the hon. member as recorded in Hansard of May 7, 1946, at page 1311. These words, marked by eloquence, were clearly and sincerely the views of the hon. gentleman in those days; indeed, they represented the views of all hon. members who occupied the treasury benches of this country at that time. This is what the hon. gentleman said:
A land of settled government,
A land of just and old renown,
Where freedom slowly broadens down
From precedent to precedent.
That is the character of our system, the system I had in mind in using the words that appear in section 26 of the bill.
That was the Canadian Citizenship Act.
That is the system which says it is not possible at any given moment to cover the whole ambit of future civil liberties, or even those liberties as they exist at the moment, in such a way that we may not lose any of their implications or endanger possible future important liberties. The best way to deal with them is the way they have been dealt with in our legal system within the commonwealth, by recognizing that these great unwritten powers are as effective in the implicit understandings of the law, rather than being set down categorically in the form of a completely written constitution. But the methods of protection of the individual under our system, based upon British constitutional tradition, are of a different order. The protection under our system depends upon two things: first, the guarantees provided by the common law and set forth in part in Magna Charta and the Bill of Rights: and second, the fundamental democratic tradition and the British operation of parliament itself. Those are the guarantees relied upon in our system which the government believes to be the best way of guaranteeing the rights and freedom of the subject: for the fact is that while France, the United States and other countries have embedded in their constitutions specific bills of rights, I do not think we, as countries within the commonwealth, need take second place to any country in the world in the protection that historically and indeed currently is afforded to the subject.
Then he went on to say:
These have proved-
Those are the guarantees he had referred to.
-to be the most lasting and effective guarantees of human liberty the world has ever known, and I do not think we would or could gain anything by changing this basis unless we wish to swing over completely to guarantees through organic legislation of the type relied upon by other countries.
Those were the views in 1946. Those views were not restricted to the hon. member but were held quite widely. But with the passing of the years and the educative process that has proceeded whereby year by year this question was brought before parliament by various members to whom I have already referred, today we find ourselves in agreement. Indeed, we now find ourselves in the position that those who opposed now support, those who minimized now say that the present bill does not go far enough, those who
Human Rights
trod upon the suggestion that something of this kind was necessary now embrace it. Yes, it might even be said, Mr. Chairman, that the stone which so many of them rejected has become the cornerstone of their present beliefs. That is laudable. It represents the operation of the parliamentary principle.
I cannot tell you, Mr. Chairman, how pleased I am at the degree to which those principles which we have advocated throughout the years have now become the generally accepted view of the House of Commons. I think that is all to the good. I think that today, as the hon. member for Essex East said in picturing the world in which we live in the cogent and powerful words he used, we in the free world must set forth declarations of those things for which we stand and in which we believe. Communism is aggressive, communism has a philosophy, and the communist knows how to use that aggressive philosophy.
Indeed one of the results of the trip I took to commonwealth countries some years ago was this. As I visited the commonwealth countries in Asia I had propounded to me everywhere the questions, what does democracy stand for, what is its meaning? We have not explained to the world yet in understandable terms, simple, direct and effective, what the meaning of freedom is to us. To a large extent the interpretation of freedom throughout the world has been left to the communists to define and to outline. Indeed its definition has become almost the exclusive monopoly of those who do not believe in freedom.
I was persuaded, and I still am, that there is a compelling need for the western world to restate and redefine its principles, its ideals, and purposes, to the end that the world may understand. Everywhere today that interpretation is based on what the communists, aggressively operating to enthrall and control the hearts of men, define it to be. Indeed, as far as free enterprise is concerned, a principle upon which our country stands, the definition in the back areas of countries within the commonwealth is the definition of the action of the moneylenders who two or three generations ago made an advance to an ancestor of a person now living there and that person still bears the responsibility of repaying a debt which ought to have been long since discharged by death. In other words, we need something to define the things in which we believe.
The reason that the United States did not have a bill of rights in its declaration of independence was simply that it was not believed to be necessary and yet when the declaration of independence came before the several legislatures of the 13 colonies one after the other they demanded that the

Human Rights
rights going back to the days ol the Mayflower declaration must be embodied within the constitution of the United States. Today we find that some 20 or more countries, believing in freedom as they do, have found it necessary to have a bill of rights. Ireland is an example; India is an example, and so I might proceed. So, sir, through the crucible of discussion we achieve something tangible.
Let me say a word regarding the special committee. I believe that more and more; if parliament is to discharge its responsibilities, we must give to committees for discussion matters such as the one which was given to this committee. The hon. member for Essex East has pointed out how effectively and how diligently the committee operated, how out of a community of counsel have been brought about changes which I would be the first to admit are beneficial. That is why the bill was submitted to a committee, and as long as I am in this position, when committees are set up as I hope they will continue to be, it is my desire in the interests of sound parliamentary government that those committees shall operate untrammelled and uncontrolled and produce to the extent possible, having regard to divergencies in membership of such committees and the difference of viewpoint, the best and most effective conclusions of which they are capable.
This committee did so. I have read all the evidence and I commend it to the members of this committee. It was a striking committee made up of members of so many different racial origins. I was impressed this morning by the words of the hon. member for Humber-St. George's when he referred to himself as a new Canadian and having the feeling that those who came here from other lands or their forebears had toward freedom and what it means. Now he is in a different position. Newfoundland has had that freedom for several hundred years but as he spoke this morning one could not but be touched by his feeling that there was that unity of purpose in the committee, irrespective of race and creed, which brought about the improvements and changes, and while the basic essence of a bill of rights has in no way been changed the bill now comes before us in a form which, as the result of the contributions of so many, certainly epitomizes the purpose and aim of a bill of rights. I will go further and say that there has been added to it the effective viewpoint of the group of dedicated members who sat on that committee.
Speaking of the preamble, I may say that almost everyone has tried to draft one. I thought it would be impossible to draft a preamble which would be exclusively related

to those things within the federal jurisdiction. I found it difficult to determine what the wording should be. However, paraphrasing the words of another, my idea of the preamble and what the bill of rights stands for could be summarized in these words:
"On these great truths we stand, and pledge by heart and under law, that God makes all men free in human dignity, whatever their colour, race or creed, to worship and to live, each equal with his neighbour; to speak his mind out clear, without reproach or fear; to tread where heroes for generations have trod, in freedom under God; on these eternal truths we pledge, by heart and under law, to keep these truths true; with all our strength to strive, and keep these truths alive".
This represents, to me, the endeavour that was made by members of this committee. The hon. member who was chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Essex West, went back 14 years to produce my suggestions in those days, and all of them are embodied in the bill of rights today. We are united now in our view that a bill of rights is necessary.
We now come to the question as to whether it is sufficient to have a statute, having regard to the constitutional difficulties which were portrayed this morning by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's. I read the evidence, and I think a summary of it is this: That a bill of rights is necessary, the experience of the past has shown that for the future; second, that as an interim measure this will be a forward step until that day when a constitutional bill of rights will be possible by agreement with the provinces. Third, as Professor Lower has pointed out, nearly every state has made some kind of formal statement of its belief in freedom sooner or later. Professor Cohen stated the need for a restatement of that which is strong in English law. He suggested the strengthening of the provision with respect to discrimination, and I welcome the wording that the committee has brought forth in this connection. He pointed out that a major policy statement on freedom is a good course to follow; that it is creative to have laws against discrimination.
I want to say this to you, Mr. Chairman. Only two years or so ago the council of churches met in Switzerland and came to the conclusion unanimously that there was nothing more beneficial to communism than the failure, anywhere in the free world, to assure equality of opportunity in the use of or in the entry into hotels, restaurants, theatres and the like. In other words, the inscription over some places which we see sometimes in our country "Patronage restricted" gives the most serious thought to those who endeavour to uphold freedom. It is a denial of the principles of freedom and

an encouragement to the communists to point out that, while we, the Christian nations, aver our belief in freedom and the brotherhood of man, we fail to practise it. However, the defence to that kind of situation will not be covered by this bill of rights because it falls within the jurisdiction of the provinces.
Professor Cohen went on to say that it will reintroduce the ideas of natural justice. He pointed out also one matter that has been referred to on a number of occasions, and that is the necessity for action being taken under the War Measures Act while we are in the days of peace, which we hope will never end. This statute went on the law books in 1914 and stayed on the law books during the period between wars. As I said recently when speaking about it. I hope the house at the next session of parliament will agree to set up a committee for the purpose of studying its principles and removing from it those features which constitute a denial of the rights of the individual without endangering the security of the state.
Now, sir, on going through the evidence I find that there is a general desire to have a constitutional amendment. I have made it quite clear that when and if, as a result of agreement amongst the provinces, Canada can in Canada amend its own constitution, then 1 would hope that the first step in the amendment of that constitution would be the preservation of our freedoms nationally in a bill of rights effective nationally and with the agreement of the provinces, without in any way interfering with those basic rights which were alluded to today by the hon. member for Bellechasse. There are going to be difficulties. It is not as simple as some say it is going to be. There have been several meetings over the years, and the last was in 1950. It is so easy to say we agree that something should be done, but it is not so easy to determine how to do that something in a manner that will be acceptable to the provinces of Canada. On January 12, 1950 the conference received the report of the committee of the attorneys general, that is the constitutional conference of the federal and provincial governments. The report contained eight resolutions which were recommended to the conference.
First of all, it recommended a grouping of the provisions of the British North America Act under six headings.
(1)	Provisions which concern parliament only. In respect of this group amendment is made and shall be made by an act of the parliament of Canada.
Human Rights
(2)	Provisions which concern the provincial legislatures only. In respect of this group amendment shall be made by an act of the provincial legislatures.
(3) Provisions which concern parliament and one or more but not all of the provincial legislatures. It was recommended that in respect of this group an act of the parliament of Canada and an act of the legislature of each of the provinces affected should be the basis of amendment.
(4) Provisions which concern parliament and all of the provincial legislatures. It was recommended in this regard that amendment should be made by an act of the parliament of Canada and acts of such majority of the legislatures and upon such additional conditions, if any, as may be decided upon. We begin to realize, Mr. Chairman, what the difficulties are when we read this last mentioned provision. There is a large field for discussion contained in those latter words.
(5)	Provisions concerning fundamental rights and the amendment of the amending procedures. In respect of this group it was suggested that provision be made for amendment by an act of the parliament of Canada and acts of the legislatures of all the provinces.
(6)	Provisions that should be repealed. There are a number of provisions in the British North America Act that in the passage of years find themselves in this category. The recommendation was that amendment procedure might be initiated by one or more of the provincial legislatures or by the parliament of Canada.
On the basis of the recommendations of the committee of attorneys general in 1950 the difficulties are underlined and most apparent. However, I must say that I was encouraged by the attitude expressed by a number of the premiers there. I recall very well that in 1946 Mr. Lesage, a member of parliament at that time, did not view with favour a bill of rights and made his contribution at the time. However, with the changing events of the years-after all, that is the basis of all progress-we now find him in the position of advancing the idea that we may have a national bill of rights. And I repeat that that viewpoint of today has to be commended.
Mr. Chairman, I think I have covered the various matters which have been dealt with here. I am not going to repeat any of the discussions of the past except those which become absolutely necessary. I simply say that this attitude of mine is not the result of the prodding by any of the provinces. It is the culmination of a national demand

Human Rights
which in consequence of changing public opinion through the years now places various legislators in our country in a position where in keeping with the views of today they have discarded the views of yesterday.
I will say no more excepting once more to say of this committee that great responsibilities were placed on its membership. They, in keeping with the finest traditions of parliament, entered into the spirit of discharging that heavy responsibility and have brought back to us the result of their thinking, based on the evidence before them and their own viewpoint, without in any way changing the essence of the bill of rights which was placed in their trust for further consideration.

Mr. Chairman, some of the witnesses before the committee made the point that there should be some inclusion in this legislation of economic rights, and I would think that clause 1 is an appropriate place to enunciate such economic rights. It seems to me that there should be stated in a bill of rights that an individual has the right of employment.
It may be said that it is difficult to enforce economic rights, that it is difficult to make provision for them. Nevertheless, as our society develops, I think it becomes more and more clear that it is essential that we set forth certain basic economic rights for our citizens. I think that would include the right of employment, the right to have a job if one is willing to work. That kind of a right is not available to Canadians at this time.
Does this include the right to work, and under what conditions?

I was just about to come to that. The hon. member can argue that point, but before the committee an endeavour was made at various times to have clauses amended in order to set forth certain basic rights. I think the hon. member's observation has a particular connotation and what I have in mind is the right of an individual to a job, an opportunity to work if he wishes to.
This whole measure is one which sets forth certain principles, and we hope those principles will be applied in a fair manner in the future. But they should not be confined, in our opinion, to merely the general rights set forth in this measure. Therefore I would like to move:
That clause 1 of the bill be amended by adding after the word "liberty" in line 1 of subparagraph (a) the following words "employment at a fair and equitable remuneration".

The purpose of this amendment would be to place in the bill of rights the declaration that Canadians should have the right to employment at fair and equal remuneration, that there should be no discrimination attached to remuneration and that remuneration from employment should be at fair rates.
The government is going to argue against this proposal. We would expect them to do that. I expect that this kind of proposal will meet with great resistance, but I am just as convinced that though it may receive opposition today, in the years to come we shall place in a bill of rights of this country certain basic economic freedoms. The way to bring that day nearer is to start now promoting certain basic concepts of economic rights and therefore it is my pleasure to move this amendment.
I rise primarily for direction. I thought we were still on the general discussion. Maybe we still are.
On clause 1.

Yes, but there is usually a general discussion on clause 1. I may tell the hon. member for Assiniboia right away that I fully support this amendment though I believe it does not come in the proper place. But the first thing, Mr. Chairman, is whether we are still on the general discussion and if so whether on the general discussion it is open to us to propose amendments.
Oh.
The hon. member says "oh". I wish it were as easy as that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand the practice has been to permit general discussion on clause 1 but I do not think the practice has been to make a complete distinction between having a general discussion and moving amendments if hon. members wish to move amendments. Once an amendment has been moved I think discussion should be confirmed to that amendment until the matter has been disposed of but, afterward, other general remarks can be made.

In other words, Mr. Chairman, you are saying that your interpretation of our procedure is that while we are on the general discussion it is open to an hon. member to move an amendment to a particular clause, providing that there may be more general discussion later if hon. members wish. I do not object to that. I just wanted to understand the situation clearly. I had always understood that at this point there was a general discussion, and that when that general discussion was over the

chairman so indicated. Then we would be ready to consider the clauses as such. But I have no objection to this procedure.
Then why this intervention?
You will see. We have some views about the inadequacy of clause 2. We wanted to do it now but we-
But we were first.

The hon. member says he was first. If he was a member of the committee he did not attend many of the meetings of that committee. As the hon. member for Charlotte pointed out, the amendments introduced by the Liberal party on this and other social points were in advance of his own. Perhaps the hon. member was not aware of that, or perhaps he became aware of it after he had read the evidence of the committee.
Do not be so tender.

I am not being tender. I am being forthright.
I am commenting, now, on the amendment and I am indicating that we support this particular amendment though I suggest there is a more appropriate place for it in a subsequent clause as I shall indicate later on. But I want the members of the committee to know, as I said in my statement in chief, and as the Leader of the Opposition indicated, that when we are talking about human rights and fundamental freedoms we must take into account the character of our times. The basic human rights and fundamental freedoms which are generally referred to as absolutes in clause 1 of the bill are that kind of rights and freedoms which have been recognized for centuries and incorporated in charters of rights and notably emphasized in legislation in the nineteenth century.
But we in this party, as the Leader of the Opposition has pointed out, recognize that political liberty, freedom of the press, freedom of assembly, valuable and essential though they are, are only part of the kind of concepts in the field of human rights that must now be recognized. I would think, as Franklin Roosevelt said, as Mackenzie King said, and as the Leader of the Opposition has so often said, that in this twentieth century when we have subscribed to the declaration on human rights, as this country did in 1948, along with some 80 nations, and when that declaration deals not only with political and legal liberties but, as well, with social and economic objectives, there is no reason why in a bill of rights when we are declaring what those rights are, we should not deal with matters that touch the economic and social welfare of the mass of the people of this country.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? He has mentioned the declaration of human rights, the international declaration of 1948. Why was that never submitted to parliament? Was not the explanation given that it contained reference to economic rights which were within the jurisdiction of the provinces? Was that not the answer?
The Prime Minister, I am sure, does not intend to create a red herring-

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: No, I am just asking a question.

I am saying that in asking that question I am sure the Prime Minister does not wish to introduce a red herring into this discussion. The fact is that the declaration on human rights, the subject of discussion in the United Nations for almost ten years, was a result of contributions made by many people, and in Canada the Canadian contribution was made under the direction and under the policy of the Leader of the Opposition who happened at that time to be in charge of matters having to do with external policy, including the United Nations. But since the right hon. gentleman has asked me a question, let me ask him one in this context.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: After you have answered mine.
I have answered your question.
Oh.

There was nothing to prevent the right hon. gentleman rising in his place at any time during the period when he was so feverish about these rights and making a motion-a supply motion-or resorting to any of the procedures which are open to ingenious members of parliament, than whom there are few more ingenious than the right hon. gentleman. But advantage was not taken of that. My own comment is not valuable, but perhaps neither comment is valuable, though the Prime Minister put forward the most invaluable comment. But I am sure the Prime Minister cannot fail to recognize the value of the concept employed in this particular method.
It may be said that equitable remuneration is a matter which involves property and civil rights. That cannot be sensibly argued, because we clearly envisage in this bill that we shall only touch those matters which come within the competence of the federal parliament, though we do not use that precise language. But there is no reason why we cannot have minimum wage legislation in the

Human Rights
federal parliament. The Prime Minister looks at me with wonderment. I repeat that there is no reason why we in the federal parliament cannot provide a basic minimum wage for those people who work in those areas that come within the competence of the federal parliament. That is what I said and it is not something that should occasion the surprise which the Prime Minister manifests.
We support this particular amendment. We suggest it has been put in the wrong section but to give an indication of our intention I make this declaration now. I would ask hon. members to consider the initiative taken by the hon. member for Fort William, the initiative taken by the hon. member for Humber -St. George's, the initiative taken by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont, and if I may refer to it the initiative taken by the modest and quiet hon. member for Essex East.

Mr. Chairman, I am surprised at the remarks of the hon. member for Essex East in his complaint that it was not proper to move an amendment on clause 1 at this time when he thought a general discussion was still in progress. For the sake of comparison let me point out to him that during the extensive discussion on clause 1 of the combines bill one of the hon. member's colleagues, the hon. member for Ottawa West, jumped in and moved an amendment just as was done now. For the sake of consistency the hon. gentleman should not complain in this instance as was indicated by the hon. member for Assiniboia.
During the course of the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia some hon. members raised questions by way of interjection. I may not be correct in my conclusion and if I am not I should like to be corrected, but I concluded that when reference was made to the rights of employees hon. gentlemen were thinking in terms of the so-called right to work laws existing in some of the states of the United States and which have been advocated in some reactionary quarters in Canada. I do not know if that is what was in the minds of hon. gentlemen who posed questions.
I believe I would be in order to express my thoughts about how the rights of individual workmen have been abrogated by certain types of union security clauses in collective agreements. I feel I am in order in doing so because of the nature of this clause and the amendment moved thereto. Some of these types of union security clauses abrogate the rights of the individual. As far as provincial jurisdiction is concerned those rights will continue to be abrogated. If the amendment becomes law I do not know what

will be the effect on agreements under federal jurisdiction. Since discussion of the bill of rights has been a lawyer's paradise I would not venture to guess what the effect on these contracts would be although I think it would have some.
There are a number of different union security provisions. In general terms they range from the closed shop which is a system demanding that an individual belong to a union before he is able to gain employment in the industry or firm with which the union has the agreement. The next is the union shop agreement which provides that an employer can hire whoever he wishes but the new employee must become a member of the union within a certain period of time varying with the contract. Next down the scale is the so-called Rand formula developed by Mr. Justice Rand, I believe in the automobile industry strike in 1946 or 1947. In general it indicates that all employees of an employer while they need not join a union in a certain period following the commencement of their employment are nevertheless required to pay an amount equal to union dues. The next in order of desirability on the part of union negotiators is the maintenance of membership principle under which if a man joins a union he must maintain membership in it during the life of the contract. At the bottom of the scale is the so-called open shop arrangement in which there is no provision whatever contained in the collective agreement regarding membership in the union. Under this system we sometimes have voluntary revocable checkoff which is a deduction of union dues which the employer makes and sends to the union.
Some of these types of union security abrogate the rights of the individual and the operation and enforcement of some other types do the same thing. I will enumerate those types and the objection to them I have. I do not think the objectionable ones are beneficial to anyone. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I desire to look briefly at the historical development of unions and the reasons for these types of union security provisions. I think we will all agree without hesitation that in the early days, before any extensive union organization was even thought of, an employee in many instances could be and in many instances was summarily fired from his employment without reason, but especially if the individual had any interest in or had shown any interest in or took any active part in the organization of any union. Many of the people in the industry who undertook to participate in union organization were in effect blacklisted. I am not too sure whether some of these black lists do not still exist today. A blacklist was a circularization of a man's name among employers, particularly employers in the same industry, that that individual was on the blacklist for union activities. When that took place his possibilities of getting employment anywhere in that industry were practically hopeless. I appreciate, Mr. Chairman, that you are wondering as to the relevancy of this to the amendment but it deals with employment.
I am giving a short background as to how we got union security provisions in the collective agreements and how these might abrogate the rights of certain individuals. Unions, therefore, thought that their members required some protection and came to the conclusion that if they had the right to control the hiring of employees then they

Human Rights
would overcome this blacklisting. Consequently, out of that arose the closed shop. All this did in some instances was to substitute the action of the union to discriminate against the individual for what was formerly the activity of the employer in discriminating against the individual, for this, and other reasons, and, I have absolutely no use for closed shop provisions where the control of hiring is in the hands of a union agent, and where the same sort of discrimination can be practised as was practised before by the employer but for different reasons. This I think is an abrogation of an individual's right to employment.
There are certain other types of union security provisions under which a person's employment is in jeopardy. If he forgos his membership in a union under certain circumstances; under the union shop provision, for argument's sake, the union itself may have the right under its constitution to remove the person's union membership from him for a variety of reasons, some of which may not be very sound; but in the process of removing that individual's union membership they also remove his right to employment if his right to employment is tied to union membership. Under certain circumstances where the union takes the initiative in removing and cancelling a person's membership I do not think it should by subsequent action, in fact, have his employment terminated accordingly.
We in the I.W.A. have a provision which says that anyone who is a member of the communist, fascist or nazi parties may not belong to our union, and that if a person who is such a member does belong to the union and this is subsequently discovered his membership can be cancelled. If this occurs and if, for argument's sake, the union has a provision, which it has a perfect right to have, to restrict membership to people with certain ideas, and they subsequently discover that there is a member in their union who is also a member of the communist party, and if action is taken within the union to cancel his membership, it should not automatically follow that he loses his employment thereby. We have enshrined this provision in our constitutional structure, in the union shop provision, and I had an active participation in it a few years ago, to the point where we indicated that this would not interfere with a person's right to employment, nor do I think it should.
We could get involved, of course, in a number of variations and different applications and that sort of thing, but I thought it would be well to express these views at this time not only because I believe in these

things, as I have said a number of times before, but when the hon. member for Assini-boia moved his amendment and got certain queries from hon. members opposite as to what he was getting at. Without embarking into another field, on the so-called right to work laws, which I have no use for either,
I think they are being misconstrued for something which they are not. I think if unions and management take the approach that I have suggested with respect to that which I have just enunciated in brief form,
I think there will be no reason to advocate so-called right to work laws.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
In connection with the amendment itself, Mr. Chairman, it is not one that the government can accept for a variety of reasons. The first reason, of course, is that this is a reversion to the attempt made in the special committee to change the form of our bill of rights from a general bill of rights into a bill of particulars and, further, to transform it from a bill of rights dealing with political rights and individual freedoms in the generally accepted sense of those words into a charter of economic rights.
There is no use beating around the bush about this matter. We have stated and stated
Human Rights
quite clearly that we did not make any attempt to make this a charter of economic rights, which would be an entirely separate sort of document dealing with an entirely different field from the field dealt with by a bill of rights. The time may come when that sort of charter should be introduced but that is not the attempt made here.
As I have said, we had in the special committee an attempt to change the bill of rights from a bill of rights into a bill of particulars. There were 22 separate amendments suggested mostly by members of the Liberal party, it is true. As I recall, the C.C.F. did not move a single amendment in the committee. I would point out that if those amendments had been adopted the subparagraphs would have gone up to (z) and we would have had to go back to (aa). As I said in the committee, I pity the school children who would be supposed to memorize a bill of rights when it was that kind of bill of particulars, which is not at all appropriate to the kind of document we are enacting. That is only one objection.
Another objection is that whatever the hon. member for Essex East or others may say about the proposed amendment, it does get us into the field of provincial jurisdiction. Whatever words you may put in the preamble indicating your intention to confine the bill to federal jurisdiction, it is, as I understand it, a law of interpretation that if, notwithstanding an expression of intent in a preamble, you introduce into that part of the bill that has legislative effect a provision which clearly goes beyond the intention expressed in the preamble then it is the section of the bill itself to which effect shall be given and not the words of the preamble.
Therefore, no matter how much we hedge it around by declarations of intent in a preamble, if in clause 1 or any of the other clauses of the bill we legislate on matters which are clearly within provincial competence the courts could not avoid saying that parliament intended to get into the provincial field and you would therefore likely have the result that the bill or part of the bill would be held to be ultra vires. We do not intend to legislate in the field of provincial competence for reasons which have been discussed exhaustively in the house and in the special committee, and for that reason in addition we cannot accept the amendment.
If anyone is in some doubt whether or not this is really a matter within provincial competence may I refer them and the hon. member for Essex East particularly to the opinion expressed by his leader on September 5, 1958 when, as Leader of the Opposition, he was discussing this sort of question in the house. At that time he was discussing the

Human Rights
applicability in Canada of the universal declaration of human rights, and he used these words as found on page 4648 of Hansard:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Yes, I think I am right that the declaration has been accepted. If I am wrong I will be corrected. It took some years, but I think it eventually was accepted by Canada. In any event, our hesitation in respect of this declaration, and I know something about this, arose from the fact that it included matters that were strictly within provincial jurisdiction. Therefore it could not be accepted with propriety by the Canadian delegation without having all of the provinces accept at least those parts of it which entrenched on provincial jurisdiction, and that was not done by all the provinces.
The very sort of provision which in those remarks the Leader of the Opposition recognized as being within provincial jurisdiction is this sort of provision relating to the right to work the sort of provision contained in article 23 of the universal declaration which reads as follows:
23(1). Everyone has the right to work, to free choice of employment, to just and favourable conditions of work and to protection against unemployment.
That provision was sought to be inserted in the bill of rights by the hon. member for Essex East in the special committee. So, Mr. Chairman, it is obvious that this kind of provision, inevitably embracing as it does provincial jurisdictions, is not the kind of provision that we can insert into the federal, the Canadian bill of rights.
I think I have given sufficient reasons why it should not be inserted here. I indicated in the committee our reaction to this sort of proposal, that this sort of proposal is a statement of objectives. Certainly it is desirable that everybody should have the opportunity to work. We accept that as a statement of objective. We have accepted that by our agreement with the universal declaration of human rights as well as by other means, but this is a statement of objective to be implemented by other specific measures. That is why I say it is not part of a bill of rights which is a statement of basic human rights and fundamental freedoms. It is that kind of document and not a charter of specific economic privileges which would require to be followed up by specific enactments in the economic field in so far as we could do it within our jurisdiction.
