speechtext:
I think we might as well meet this argument head on, because the minister is repeating the technique used in the committee and undoubtedly will register his objection to any proposal of this character. First of all, on the question of

the competence of parliament, my hon. friend says that if the amendment moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia were allowed to become integrated into clause 1 (a) it would be clear that the courts would rule this to be outside the competence of parliament notwithstanding the limitation in the preamble. I do not agree, first of all, with that statement because the preamble, under the rules of interpretation, may be used by the courts to determine the meaning of a section or of a word in a section.
If my hon. friend's argument had any validity, that validity would also have been present before there was any agreement by the administration to include a preamble in the bill, and when the bill was before us on second reading. There was no preamble at that time containing a phrase that suggested the limitation of federal competence under section 91. There was nothing in clause 2 that in any way limited the word "property" or the word "Canada". When we argued that the word "Canada" and the word "property" in section 2 were, as Mr. Louis Philippe Pigeon stated, a violation of provincial powers, the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister argued to the contrary. I clearly stated in the house and in the committee that there was no doubt as to what the intention of the Prime Minister was. He intended the clause to touch on those matters that came within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. I did state that the courts would not interpret what we said in this house, they would look at the wording of the bill. Notwithstanding that my hon. friend, when there was no preamble, when there was no thought of limitation on the words, argued that the words in the form in which they were presented did not lend themselves to the construction which he kept putting forward. Now my hon. friend cannot have both positions taken in different contexts.
I say to him that, assuming there was validity in what he said, and I do not agree that there was, and assuming that this limitation of powers has got to be in an operative part of the bill, we could put in an operative part of the bill, right in this clause, a clear indication that what is proposed in this amendment relates only to what is within the competence of the federal parliament. There could be no doubt about that. I would suggest that could be done, if it is necessary. I do not believe it will have to be done because the courts will look at the intention stated in the preamble, and particularly the French text which is unambiguous.
The second point that my hon. friend has met headlong is one we are going to have

to meet, of course, in the future with regard to another proposal which the Leader of the Opposition has in mind in another context. My hon. friend says this is a declaration of rights, and what is proposed in the amendment by the hon. member for Assiniboia is a bill of particulars.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: The statements of my hon. friend are, I am afraid, so erroneous that I cannot allow them to go without reply, especially if this question is going to arise again. I should like to establish it on a proper basis, and not on the erroneous basis on which the hon. member for Essex East has just left it. With respect to this matter of federal competence, I said that I did not think there was any need for a preamble saying that we were only legislating within the field of federal competence because I said we have drafted a bill in connection with matters only within the federal competence. We had been careful in the drafting of this bill not to get out of the field of federal competence and into the field of provincial authority. I suggested, therefore, that I did not believe a preamble was necessary from that point of view, but if my hon. friends were more impressed by the opinion of those who appeared before the committee then, in order to remove any element of uncertainty in the bill, I would say put in a preamble which makes it clear we are legislating only within the federal competence. speechtext: No, I agree.

That is what my hon. friend was saying I had said. Notwithstanding that we have a preamble containing the clearest expression of intention, which I think we have, and notwithstanding that we are enlarging the bill of rights as now drawn to include subjects which are within provincial competence, then it does not matter what we said in the preamble, the courts will look at the statute we have enacted and will have to deal with it on that basis. I say again that in the bill of rights as we drafted it and as it came out of the committee there is nothing in the legislative portions which steps outside the field of federal competence.
_ With regard to property there is no question that there are aspects of property within federal competence. Not all property rights are reserved to the provinces under section 92. Section 92 makes it clear that the only property rights within the jurisdiction of the

Human Rights
provinces are exactly those. Section 13 gives to the provinces jurisdiction over property and civil rights in the provinces. So that makes it quite clear, if further clarity were necessary, that in respect of those heads under section 91 which have any aspect of property connected with them, property in those aspects is within the federal field of competence.
Therefore it is appropriate for us to use words in the bill of rights, as we did, referring to the "enjoyment of property". Any property rights contained in the bill as it came out of the committee would be interpreted by the courts as matters coming within the federal field of jurisdiction, and I think the preamble makes clear our intention. If we accepted what the opposition invited us to insert into the bill we would be in many cases putting in matters within provincial jurisdiction, and we would have a bill of rights not confined to the federal field at all. The question of employment is a field within the provincial jurisdiction. I would say at once without fear of contradiction that it is a field within provincial jurisdiction far more than within federal jurisdiction, that it cannot be accepted by this parliament, and that this government, with its respect for the constitution, is not prepared to accept it.

Surely it is not too much to say that in 1960 we should have in a Canadian bill of rights the declaration that a person should have the right to employment. The government of course would be in contempt of this bill of rights if this were there, because half a million Canadians could prove that the bill of rights did not apply to them, at least until such time as the government had taken further action.

We might have to go up to the letter "z" and then look at the poor school children he said who study the bill. Is this a valid reason on which to found an argument to exclude a section which says that Canadians should have the right to employment at a fair and reasonable remuneration?
My understanding of the bill of rights in the main as far as school children are concerned is that we should put a preamble in the bill which would be in picturesque and imaginative language and that it was the preamble which would hang in the schools, and that the school children would probably study that part of the bill of rights and not the bill of rights in all its detail. Even if we made it slightly more difficult for students because we added another clause, surely that is no reason to set aside the proposition that it is time in this country that we said people should have the right to employment at a fair and equitable remuneration.
The minister said that if this were put in the bill the courts would declare it ultra vires. No one will say that the question of fair and equitable remuneration is entirely a federal jurisdiction; but also no one will surely say that the federal government has not some authority, some responsibility, in the field of employment.
Mr. Chairman, we put this forward because we think it would strengthen the bill of rights. We think the bill of rights without any economic provision will allow many people who have no visible means of support because they have no jobs to go on in this condition without the federal government going at least so far as to set forth in the bill of

rights that Canadians should have the right to employment at a fair and equitable remuneration.
Even if the government should vote down this amendment, that does not kill the idea. In my view it is just as essential to have economic rights as it is to have other rights. The two go together; they are inseparable. We feel that economic rights can best be achieved when we have protection as defined in this bill; but we suggest that this bill is not complete and that it should be made more complete by the inclusion of such an amendment.

Mr. Chairman, we had some discussion of this question in the committee, and it was the question of whether the form of a declaration was any the less positive law, any less effect as an enacting law than the form of words without a declaration.
With respect to Mr. Mundell and' other witnesses who put forward this view, my considered opinion is it is not only not weaker in the form of a declaration but indeed it is stronger. After all, every enactment by parliament is a declaration. We could put into the bill of rights the provision that every person has the right to freedom of religion. Is this any the less law if it is stated that it is hereby declared that every person in Canada has the right to freedom of religion? Of course, it is not any the less law; indeed, it is a stronger enactment of the law because the declaration strengthens it by taking it out of the rule against the retrospective operation of statutes, and it is our declared intention to have this bill of rights have a retrospective effect and application with respect to statutes

now on the books. I submit, therefore, that the declaration form is stronger than the form of the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Essex East.
In support of my view, may I remind the committee that the British North America Act itself uses the form of declaration in section 91 which outlines those subjects upon which it is competent for the parliament of Canada to legislate, where it says:
And for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms of this section, it is hereby declared that (notwithstanding anything in this act) the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated.
And the courts have passed upon this ever since 1867, and never has the question been raised that the form of words "it is hereby declared" has the force of a legislative enactment, so I am not able to accept the amendment.

We think that "due process of law", being a phrase of ancient and honourable lineage in English common law going back to 1335 and having received interpretations in the United States courts which have had beneficial results there, as was admitted by Professor Cohen, that notwithstanding the doubts that have been expressed, the better opinion is that there are more advantages in the phrase "due process of law" than in the alternative phrases that have been suggested.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
I just want to add that the evidence before the committee clearly established that the phrase "due process of law", while not entirely unknown to Anglo-Canadian law having been mentioned in a statute of Edward II, has not for a long time been in current use in our jurisprudence. We

Human Rights
have relied on the English practice and we recognize "according to law" or "according by law" or "in accordance with law", following the usages in United Kingdom courts as a means of expressing what in the United States legal system they understand by due process. Due process is recognized in the United States constitution and it has been subjected to different interpretations in hundreds of cases in that country. It means different things in different jurisdictions. While our courts are not obligated to regard United States decisions as authoritative, and while I recognize that United States decisions, in the absence of Canadian judgments, may be regarded as persuasive, the fact is that by the use of "due process" in this context and in this unusual way we are imposing upon our courts an obligation to begin a new Canadian jurisprudence.
This is not the case in Canadian law with regard to the suggested phrase "in accordance with law" or "by law" or the other phrase I mentioned a moment ago. I hope that the minister has been impressed with the evidence on this point and I hope that he will give consideration to the amendment before the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
I should like to indicate that we have an open mind when we first give consideration to these things but after giving consideration to them and giving due weight to the points of view that are advanced by others who are concerned with the matters involved we come to a conclusion as to what is the best course to follow. Then I am not able to convince myself I would be acting in accordance with my duties if I were to tell parliament that I agree to some course I did not think was the best course. We believe the phrase "due process of law" is the best phrase in this context for the purpose we have in mind.

speechtext:
Before we deal with paragraph (b), it is noteworthy that the original paragraph of clause formerly 2 (b), read as follows:
(b)	the right ol the individual to protection of the law without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex;
The paragraph now reads:
(b) the right of the individual to equality before the law and the protection of the law;
The discriminatory feature has been pushed up, pursuant to suggestions that were made from this party, to clause 1, and there has been added to paragraph (b) the phrase, "equality before the law". The minister will recall the discussion on this point. It was felt by the government that the amendment,

we proposed, the phrase "protection of the law without discrimination" etc., did not strengthen the clause to the extent which it was felt was desirable. The minister did accept the suggestion that the phrase "equality before the law", which I think very considerably strengthens that subsection, did strengthen the subsection.
I would simply observe that with regard to the other rights mentioned, those are all absolutes in form but we have assumed that they carry with them qualifications now provided for in our law. None of these are really absolute freedoms. Indeed the minister made the observation in committee that it was envisaged, for instance, in the case of freedom of the press that did not mean licence of the press, and I fully agree. Having noted that they are absolutes, it should not be forgotten, with regard to the suggestion that was made earlier in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Assini-boia and the amendments that were moved by this party in the committee, they, too, need not be regarded as absolutes but could be regarded for what they are as a declaration of particular human rights, with obvious qualifications, which I should have thought would make it possible for the government to readily accept the suggestions which we did introduce based upon the various provisions in the declaration on human rights.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the fundamental freedoms specified in clause 1 seem to deal in one way or another principally with the protection of the individual from the state. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's:
That clause 1 be amended as follows; That the following paragraph, to be designated paragraph
(c), be added after the present paragraph (b):
"The right of the Individual to the protection of the law against arbitrary interference with privacy, family, home, or correspondence, and against attacks upon his honour and reputation." and that the remaining paragraphs be relettered accordingly.
This amendment to clause 1 puts the state in a much more favourable light by declaring that the individual also possesses certain rights and protection by the state. This particular amendment deals with the protection that the state provides against wrongs that may be inflicted upon any one individual by other individuals, which may be inflicted in the course of ordinary social relationships. One would expect and hope that the honour of a man and the beliefs he holds would be a guide and inspiration to him in everything he says and does; hence the advancement of this particular amendment which I think is an important one.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, here again we have a matter which was discussed fully in the special committee. The hon. members opposite made an attempt there, as they do now, to insert the general provisions of article XII of the universal declaration into the Canadian bill of rights. I can only say once again, repeating what I said in the committee, that most of what they have in mind is already covered in the wording of our bill of rights, which again serves to establish the adequacy of the draftsmanship of our bill of rights.
What do they ask? They ask that we particularize with respect to the right of the individual to the protection of the law against arbitrary interference with privacy, family, home, or correspondence. May I point out that this bill really declares that there exist in Canada the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property. If you have the right to security of the person you are protected then against arbitrary interference with privacy. If you have the right to security you are protected against arbitrary interference with your family, and also against arbitrary interference with your home. Our bill goes on to say that a person has the right to the enjoyment of property. If he has the right to the enjoyment of property he is protected against arbitrary interference with correspondence, which is another particular which this amendment seeks to introduce. So I say with respect to the first four particulars of this amendment that they are already covered in the present bill of rights.
Then the amendment goes on to deal with what I suggest are really matters in the field of private rights, the question of rights as between individuals. The hon. member for Fort William in moving this amendment, when he came to that part of it which deals with attacks upon "his honour and reputation" made it clear that he was thinking there of an attack by one individual upon the honour and reputation of another individual. That is why I say that here he is dealing with the field of private rights. That is the sort of thing which is covered by the law of torts, the law of libel, slander and so on. That again is not the sort of thing to write into a bill of rights dealing with the basic rights and fundamental freedoms of the individual in the over-all political sense in which we are using those terms here. That is a matter which has always been left to the operation of private law, the law of torts, in the way I have described.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
The uncertainties were caused by the use of certain words. The words "due process" create great uncertainty because they do not have in our jurisprudence the settled meaning they have in a varied way in the United States. The hon. gentleman cannot therefore address as an answer to the argument of the hon. member for Fort William the proposition that there is now in the law that method for the protection of those rights. Arbitrary interference with privacy, with the family, home, corre-spondance are all capable of protection under the existing law. All we do when we say freedom of assembly, freedom of the press is to declare not something new but to reaffirm what we say in the preamble, what we

recognize to be the present law, and that present law is determined in the case of freedom of religion in the two Saumur cases. The hon. member for Bellechasse reminds me that there is a second case on now in which there is some argument as to the exclusive competence of the federal government in the field of religion. The question of the freedom of the press, yes. My hon. friend the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont points out that the case to which the hon. member for Bellechasse directed our intention was before Judge Lizotte who said:
(Translation):
Justice Lizotte does not share that opinion. According to him, freedom of religion falls into the category of civil rights, a category which, under the constitution, is restricted to the provinces. The plaintiffs also claimed that the act being infringed came under criminal law, because penalties were provided for offences.
(Text):
It is clear, therefore, that the fundamental law of the land deals with the situation. The fundamental law of the land deals with the rights which the hon. member for Fort William has sought to have us protect, and all that we are doing is to ask that there should be a recognition in the law by way of a declaration against arbitrary interference with privacy, against the family, against the home, correspondence and attacks upon one's honour and reputation. This is a declaration against molestation, in part, and molestation is one of those rights which Sir Frederick Pollock thought the common law did not adequately deal with, and that was later followed by the decision in the Christie case where there was an attempt to define the matter more clearly.
There is one further argument that is incorporated in this amendment of the hon. member for Fort William. We have recognized in the preamble the importance of the home and the family in Canadian society. We say in the first paragraph of the preamble:
The parliament of Canada, affirming that the Canadian nation is founded upon principles that acknowledge the supremacy of God, the dignity and worth of the human person and the position of the family in a society of free men and free institutions;
We recognize this right in the preamble, as we do the human rights and fundamental freedoms in this bill. Should we not take advantage, then, of declaring that one of the rights in this bill of rights is the existence of the home-le foyer-the family, the solid basic elemental institution in our society? That is the purport of part of this amendment and I had hoped that the minister himself who, I am sure, in principle, shares our concern in this matter would recognize the validity of our proposal. This is relevant to

a declaration on human rights. Again I remind the hon. gentleman of the strong arguments that he made in committee. As he told the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and other members of the committee, he could not take out "torture", he could not take out "cruel, inhuman and degrading" because that would put the Canadian government in an invidious position vis-a-vis the declaration on human rights. He reminded us that the Soviet union would say of us that we were accepting lesser terms in our bill of rights than we were in the declaration on human rights. Well, the declaration on human rights says:
No one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with his privacy, family, home or correspondence nor to attacks on his honour or reputation. Everyone has the right to the protection of the law against such interference or attack.
So I would urge the minister to reconsider his position and to recognize that there could be no harm result from the inclusion of this kind of declaration. It will be notice to all and sundry that this nation of free people recognizes the validity and the solid basis of the family as a vital factor in the Canadian nation. That seems to me to be an argument that ought to impress the government and I had hoped it would.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman overlooks the fact that in seeking to introduce this amendment restricting the protection of the law to particulars he would, as I see it, cut down the extent of the protection provided under subparagraph (a), because that subparagraph without restriction says an individual has the right to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property and the right not to be deprived thereof except by due process of law. The individual enjoys those rights without restriction. Without inhibition, he enjoys them in every aspect of his life as an individual.
Now the hon. gentleman seeks to introduce a limitation. He seeks to introduce a particularization and say: This right applies only to protection against arbitrary interference with privacy, or family, or home or correspondence; that is the field within which we want these rights to operate. We want them to operate in general, in toto with respect to all aspects of the life and being of the individual. How can it possibly be seriously argued that if an individual has a right to security of the person he is not protected in his family life?
The family is a group of individuals and each one of them has the right to the security of the person and the enjoyment of property. Therefore the family as a unit enjoys the sum total of all the rights of the individual who make up that family, rights that we have 79951-0-470
Human Rights
ensured in this bill. We do not want these rights to be confined within the narrow limits that the hon. member seeks to set out each time he introduces another particular. The effect would be to weaken, not to strengthen the provisions contained in this measure. Our bill of rights is better in that it does not limit the protection that the individual enjoys or that the family enjoys as a group of individuals enjoying the collective rights that every one of us as an individual enjoys.
With regard to the final parts of the amendment, protection against attacks on honour and reputation, again I can only say that they are subject to law now. In this respect we are not doing anything, but these are under provincial laws. Does the hon. gentleman suggest we can enact a federal law against ordinary libel and slander? It is the law of libel and slander that gives the power to protect against infringement of these rights. Most certainly it is. We have no power to enact a law of libel or slander.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: We are not enacting; we are just declaring. Surely that is the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
This, I think, is revealing exactly the difference between us and the opposition. They want us to declare a law with respect to rights that the federal parliament has no power to protect because we have no power to enact laws of libel and slander. Therefore, what on earth is the point of our legislating and saying there are rights of protection in the field of libel and slander? We have no power over that. My hon. friend would have a hollow, empty declaration, a great many hollow words meaning nothing, if we followed' his policy.
That is not the kind of bill of rights we want. We want a bill of rights within the federal field of competence declaring rights that attach to the individual which this parliament has the power to ensure can attach to him so that parliament can see that he gets the full protection of those rights. That is why we have set our faces against all these efforts to introduce meaningless, hollow phrases which would be a shallow puff trying to pretend to the people that you are doing something you know perfectly well you cannot do for them.

Mr. Chairman, I propose to move an amendment to clause 1. I know that the Minister of Justice will characterize my action in this regard as particularizing; yet I believe that there are some rights which should be included in the present bill which are not included. I believe that individuals in Canada should have the right to move from one area to another and the right to live within any area within the confines of their own country. Surely such a right is fundamental to the happiness and well-being of Canadian citizens to live in a free society. These rights are not accorded to citizens all over the world. Perhaps there are times in our own country when we have felt that these rights were not accorded to our own citizens. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Fort William:
That the following paragraph, to be designated paragraph (c) be added after the present paragraph (b):
"The right of the individual to freedom of movement and residence within the borders of Canada." and that the remaining paragraphs be relettered accordingly.

speechtext:
With respect to the amendment now moved, here again we get into a bill of particulars. What my hon. friends are now trying to write into the bill of rights is a very particular and special attribute of citizenship which, of course, if it is important to assert, should be asserted in the Canadian Citizenship Act. But this particular attribute of citizenship, the right to freedom of movement and of residence within the borders of Canada has, as I see it, no place in a general bill of rights. A general bill of rights provides that every individual has the 79951-0-470$
Human Rights

We discussed the matter of freedom in the committe and freedom does not mean licence. In the earlier subparagraphs (a) and (b) we are talking about rights, and we have conferred deliberately by subparagraph (a) the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property. If we stopped there those would be absolute rights because there would be no words of limitation. Therefore it is necessary for us to go on and provide these words, "and the right not to be deprived thereof except by due process of law", which means that a person who would otherwise have an absolute right to liberty and security of the person is nevertheless liable to be deprived of that right if, for instance, he is convicted of a criminal offence by due process of law and therefore properly sentenced to confinement in jail.
But having accepted that approach, and my hon. friends opposite have accepted it because they have not attempted to change it and could not since it would not be possible to argue otherwise, they now seek to insert additional rights not subject to the restraint that persons are liable to be deprived of them by due process of law. You will observe, Mr. Chairman, that the right now sought to be included by this amendment is an absolute right, the right of the individual to freedom of movement and residence within the borders of Canada, an absolute and unlimited right not subject to being taken away even by due process of law.
This is one of the reasons why I object to all these attempts by my hon. friends to introduce these particulars in a place in the bill of rights after the general subclause (a) which makes it clear that the rights therein provided are to be enjoyed subject to the likelihood of being deprived of them by due process of law. It is not responsible legislation to seek to confer, as these amendments do, absolute rights in a form which would place them beyond the reach even of the ordinary processes of law. Mr. Chairman, for purposes of identification this amendment can be identified as article XV of the universal declaration of human rights, the discussion of which took place at page 633 of the report of the proceedings before the special committee on human rights and fundamental freedoms. For the reasons given at that time, but particularly for the reason that I still fail to see how Canadian law can confer upon anybody the right to acquire another nationality, I am unable to accept the amendment.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Justice is making the same argument again. This amendment is proposed by the hon. member for Fort William, who is himself a pretty good example of what those who come to Canada and accept membership in this nation can do and are contributing to this country. The hon. member for Fort William was born in Italy, has served his community the city of Fort William as mayor for a long time, and is now a very ardent, industrious and constructive member of this house. Therefore, it is appropriate that he should move this particular amendment.
The hon. member for Cartier who rose a few minutes ago is likewise one of those men whose family came from Europe, sought asylum and sanctuary and the opportunity of making their way in this country. They are the embodiment of what we are seeking to establish in a right that is recognized now in the domestic law of many European countries, and affirmed in the declaration on human rights.
Mr. Chairman, there are individuals who are what are called "heimatloss", who are without nationality, and who in some countries are denied the opportunity of nationality. There are people who come to this country from certain areas of the world who are sometimes unaware that once they have lived in this country for the prescribed period and have qualified in other respects they can become Canadian citizens. This right will not only serve to bring home this fact to such people; it will not only remove the matter of "heimatloss" in some particular situations; it will do something that will enable this country to assert vis-a-vis certain other countries the supremacy of our law in respect of people who are resident within our borders.
In Italy, in Japan and in certain other European nations the laws of the land do not allow a person to abandon his nationality. A person might come from one of those countries to Canada, might live here more than five years and become a Canadian citizen, yet according to the law of his country of origin he continues to be a national of his country of origin.
What we are asserting here, then, first of all, is the right of nationality, a right which was taken up by the man who proposed this amendment, and the right of the Canadian citizen if he so wishes to change his nationality. That is a basic right. It is a right that is not a particular, as the Minister of Justice said, any more than some of the other particularizations which he himself embodied in this bill before it reached this committee. It is not any more of a particularization than the

principles put forward by the Prime Minister and embodied in one of our amendments that was voted down and referred to by the Leader of the Opposition as one of the objectives stated by the Prime Minister. It is a right that should be included in this bill of rights and there has been no satisfactory answer by the Minister of Justice to the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS

I will give one further answer. The right to have nationality in Canada is conferred by the Canadian Citizenship Act and it exists there. All those who come to our country, no matter what may be the law of the country from which they come, enjoy that right. That exists now for Canadians on this side of the house as for Canadians on the other side of the house, all of whom have made valuable contributions, who may have come from other countries. We have them in our own ranks. The rights of acquisition of nationality is contained in the citizenship act.
I can only repeat my answer to the other parts of the amendment, and I am sorry if I do not carry conviction with the hon. member, but I cannot see how any national bill of rights can be prepared to say that the laws of Canada can provide the right to acquire the nationality of another country. That might be a proper principle to put in a universal declaration of rights but it does not seem to me appropriate to put in a national bill because our law cannot confer the right to acquire the nationality of another country.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: It seems to me that the minister has overlooked another situation, precisely the situation referred to by the hon. member for Essex East, that there are certain countries that do deny to their citizens the right to alienate their nationality for another nationality.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS

speechtext:
Perhaps the minister
would allow me to continue. I have not taken up very much time during this debate. We have never done that in this country, but there is nothing in our law to guarantee that as a right coming under our law whatsoever and it does seem to me that the amendment which has been offered by the hon. member for Fort William is putting something substantive into this bill for perhaps the first time because everything else in it is declared to be rights that have existed. Now this is a right that does not exist in any Canadian law at the present time. There just is no law in Canada which denies the right to alienate our nationality but there is nothing that says we have the right to do it.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS

speechtext: Of course it could not.

speechtext:
The minister was told by my hon. friend from Essex East that in certain countries they refuse to their natives the right to alienate their nationality. We do not refuse that right, but we do not expressly state that it is a right and my hon. friend in his amendment is expressly stating it is a right and the hope that in a really free country it will be recognized as a right, and for that reason it would seem to me that this would add additional substance to the bill.
Then there is the other consideration that all this bill is doing is saying it is hereby recognized and declared that in Canada there have existed and shall continue to exist. One of the rights that does exist in Canada under the citizenship act of which my hon. friend from Essex East was the father in this house is the right of persons who are admitted for settlement in this country to become citizens under certain conditions carefully defined. That is one of the most precious rights we offer to the people in this country, and why should we not put it in this bill of rights?

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
I think I can draw the attention of the minister to another reason why this amendment should be accepted. It is quite conceivable that at some time in the future the citizenship act might be repealed. Does the minister know, for example, there are countries in the world which do not grant citizenship to any others except those who are native born? It is conceivable that at some time some government here might decide to follow the line of reasoning of those other countries which do not grant citizenship to newcomers to their land and that is why I say that if such a government in the future gets such a viewpoint and decides to repeal the citizenship act there is nothing in our rights in Canada that will give arrivals in Canada the right to have citizenship, that precious right. To avoid such a danger I think this amendment does represent a right to which every newcomer to Canada should be entitled.
While I am on my feet I should like to say to the minister that when examining an amendment he should examine it with a view of generosity rather than niggardliness. If there is some basis for an amendment it does not matter if it is particularized a little. I think the spirit of this bill is to extend whatever rights are conceivable even if they are in the form of particularizations and therefore I appeal to the minister to
Human Rights
look on these amendments generally like a minister of justice should and give every possible favourable consideration to them.
I am sure the minister speaking from the very lofty position he occupies will not for a moment pretend that all the wisdom and all the knowledge and all the interpretation is with him. Surely he will agree that there is some capacity, some thinking, some reasoning power, some understanding of human rights on this side of the house. I do not think he should lightly set aside these amendments because they are the work of serious men, made by serious people, by thinking people not without some knowledge and experience. This is not necessarily a part measure. This is a bill on human rights which affects every member in this house and in the country and therefore I appeal to the minister to look upon these amendments in as generous a way as possible.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: I should like to ask the mover of the amendment a question suggested to me by the Joyce case in Britain. Some members may remember that Joyce, known as Lord Haw Haw, was brought back to Britain after the war and convicted and hanged for treason despite the fact that he had gone through the German citizenship courts and become a German citizen. There was a long discussion of that question of nationality at that time and as I understand it the British crown claimed that he was not in a position to eliminate his nationality. I just wondered in view of that particular case, for example, whether the hon. member who proposed this particular amendment had considered the possibility that it would mean that Canada, for example, would be precluded from trying for treason someone who might have Canadian citizenship and then had moved to another country, say an enemy country. It is not hard for us to envisage the country being an enemy and we would forfeit our rights to try this person by putting in this particular change.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: The case which the hon. member has mentioned concerned a man named Joyce who tried to divest himself of his British nationality in time of war. If I remember the case the British government said he could not do that because there was a state of war, and they acted under the defence of the realm act. Joyce offered the defence that he was not a British subject because he had taken Irish nationality previously.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with deference to the Leader of the Opposition, were not these the facts? He was travelling and maintained a British passport and therefore,

Human Rights
continuing to have a British passport, Britain owed to him certain rights, namely the right of continued protection. Because he held a British passport he could not avow another citizenship even though he contended that he was not of British citizenship. The House of Lords decided-one judge dissenting as I recall it-that anyone carrying a British passport must be presumed to be asking for the protection of the British crown and having that passport placed himself in the position of being subject to the law of treason.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps because the Prime Minister has stated part of the case I may be permitted to participate in this discussion. At that time in Britain there was no such thing as a law of nationality. There was merely the matter of status. People residing there and owing allegiance to the British monarch were British subjects. It was not until 1947, when we passed the Canadian Citizenship Act declaring in section 26 that a Canadian citizen is a British subject, that our act was followed later by the enactment of a nationality act in United Kingdom. Both the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition are partly right, but I did want to add those few words to the discussion.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to move another amendment to clause 1. This amendment deals with the position of the family in Canadian society. I believe that the family is one of the essential constituents of our society. I know that the position of the family is mentioned in the fourth line of the first paragraph of the preamble but I feel that although it is mentioned here it should be again mentioned in the body of the bill.
I know, too, that the amendment which I am going to move is also a part of the universal declaration but I do not see that that derogates from its value. I also know that I moved this amendment in the committee but again I think I still have the right to move it in this committee and to ask that it be given consideration. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Port William:
That the following paragraph to be designated paragraph (c) be added after the present paragraph (b):
"The right of the family to protection by society and the state as the natural and fundamental group unit."
and that the remaining paragraphs be re-lettered accordingly.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word in support of this amendment but before doing so I should like to say that I listened with interest as I am sure

the committee did last evening and again today to the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont who substantiated the basis of this amendment in the speech which he delivered on clause 1.
I am somewhat surprised that there would not be included in the bill a statement covering the amendment other than that statement which is now contained in the preamble. The committee will realize at once that the family is the basis of our society. It is upon the family that Canadians rely as the basis of the community. In all parts of Canada that is so. I am sure I will be pardoned if I make particular reference to what is contained in the civil code of Quebec with reference to certain rights concerning the family. If this bill is to be a truly national bill, as the Minister of Justice has repeatedly stated, surely there should be some reference in the operative part of this measure to the family as a unit.
In certain parts of our country parochial life has a very important part to play. As a matter of fact it is the family that makes up the parish. This is not exclusive to the province of Quebec but applies to many other provinces if not all. It would seem to me that a truly national bill of rights should contain some reference to the protection of the family. If this bill is to be what the government wants it to be and what the Minister of Justice has repeatedly said it should be, then it strikes me that there should be an insertion in clause 1 which would protect the rights of the family.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

Page 647 and the following pages of that report. I do not think there is very much I can add to what I said there. I wish to assure the hon. member for Cartier that I have considered all these suggested amendments extremely carefully. The fact that the majority of them have been rejected up to this point does not mean they have not been considered carefully nor does it mean that the contents thereof have not been recognized as desirable in themselves. But the reason for rejection is any one of the reasons I have given to date, that they have the right without limitation, or that it is in my mind an undesirable particularization, or some such reason.
Here we come to a case where again the rights of the family, the basic laws involved

there, particularly the context mentioned by the hon. member, are wholly or almost entirely in the provincial field, the laws governing the relation between wife and husband, parents and children and so on. That kind of family law is, I think it will be agreed, entirely provincial and not federal, so that in that aspect we are dealing with something which is exclusively provincial and not within our jurisdiction.
When you come to the question of the rights of the family in the more abstract sense, then, in my view, having considered it most carefully, the rights of the family are simply the sum total of the rights enjoyed by each individual who makes up the family, and there is no right upon which anyone may rely for the protection of his family which is not a right which attaches to him as an individual, whether it be the right of the security of the person or the enjoyment of property. If one of his children's liberties is interfered with, then the head of the family protects the right of the child, but he does it by a personal action, an action with respect to the right of the individual's security of the person. Therefore, as I say, the rights of the family in this sense are simply the sum total of all the rights of the individual who make up the family, and we have anticipated the amendment therefore by our bill of rights itself which confers upon the individual the inalienable right to life, liberty, security of the person, and enjoyment of property, and the amendment therefore adds nothing but is merely dealing with a subject that comes within provincial jurisdiction.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Mai-sonneuve-Rosemont, that clause one be amended as follows:
That the following paragraph, to be designated paragraph (c), be added after the present paragraph (b):
"The right of the individual of equal access to public service".
And that the remaining paragraphs be re-lettered accordingly.
This is a right that is embodied in the constitutions of six European nations, and was there prior to the declaration on human rights. It is a declaration that is contained in the declaration on human rights. Because of that latter fact, in view of the position taken by the Minister of Justice in the committee when we began discussing in general terms the bill before the committee, and prior to the introduction of amendments, it would seem to deny to the minister in all logic any justification for any resistance to this amendment.
Human Rights
In this free country of ours there is no doubt that, subject to citizenship, every one has the right to serve as the representative of the people in this parliament and in our legislatures and, subject to other considerations, in our municipal bodies. But every one in Canada does not recognize that that right exists.
Since the war we have brought almost two million new people to this country, and they are in themselves justification of the policies of government that made it possible for them to come here. They are making a contribution just as those of us who were born here and just as those who preceded them and who became citizens of our country by the procedure of naturalization. They have the right, and we want them to know they have the right, not only to public service in the legislature or in parliament, but to public service as servants of the crown in the government service.
We have in this country a civil service commission, and we recognize the merit system, and correctly so; but there are certain aspects of our public service in which the civil service commission does not operate, and this particular right would apply to that situation. A woman who was born in Czechoslovakia, in Poland, in Rumania, in France, or in any European nation, and whose background and conditions at home are such as to cause her to take what might be regarded as menial employment, should not be denied that opportunity simply because she belongs to a particular race or because her national origin was such that-

speechtext: Is she denied it?

speechtext: My hon. friend knows perfectly well that in certain departments of government right now it is not possible for certain people to get jobs which are at the disposal of agencies other than the civil service commission. That applies-

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS

Whatever the situation was before, if such situations do exist, now is the opportunity to correct them; but it is not only that, Mr. Chairman,-

speechtext: Has the hon. member some actual facts?

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
I refer not only to the public service in the government, not only the right to take one's place in a legislative body but to the public service

Human Rights
generally under the laws of our country. We do know-and anyone who lives in a community as I do where there are thousands of new Canadians knows-that there are situations which are covered by this very proposed right, and it applies not only to the legislature, not only to work in the public service, but to publice service of a broader aspect.
The acceptance of this amendment, which for many people is a very basic right, a basic necessity, a basic opportunity, would be a way to meet their particular problem. When the Minister of Justice tells us that one of the objectives is to have this bill of rights available in the schools so that everybody can see it and be inspired by the freedom that exists in this country I would think that this would be a right that the minister would readily accept. Think of a right like this declared under a law passed by the parliament of Canada and the effect of that on a young boy born in Italy, born in Germany, born in Czechoslovakia, born in any of the European nations. It would be an inspiration to such young people as perhaps no other right in this particular series of amendments or in the bill itself would.
I urge that this amendment be accepted. We will not forget that there have been situations in Canada where, in spite of men being elected to public office, they were not allowed to take their seats. We have the case of Mr. Hart, a Jewish gentleman in another province. We have the case of William Lyon Mackenzie, denied three times the right to take his seat in the legislative assembly of Upper Canada. These things may not happen now but we are not legislating for now, we are legislating for the future.
When I look at the hon. member for Hum-boldt-Melfort, who played a notable part in the work of the committee, I remember the words he uttered from his seat in the back row on the occasion of his first speech in the house, when he mentioned standing in front of the monument of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, proud that he was a member of this house.
I have never forgotten that moving statement of the hon. member. There are other members and other potential members like the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort. Here is an opportunity for parliament directed by the government to give that inspiration. I so move, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, there is in the universal declaration of human rights a clause which outlines the right of any individual to social security and to economic,
[Mr. Martin (Essex East) .3
social and cultural rights which are indispensable for the development of one's personality. When we realize that these rights have been in this declaration for a period of nearly ten years I think that if we are to adopt a bill of rights in the year 1960 we should add to many of the ancient rights enumerated in Bill No. C-79 some of these rights which we now enjoy but to which I think we should give recognition in order that people may be protected because we are dealing here in terms of the future.
I wish to point out that in the postwar period the constitutions and the declarations of rights of the fourth French republic, the Italian republic and the Federal Republic of Germany have been amended to incorporate some new rights such as the right to work, the right to a living wage, the right to rest and leisure, the right to all levels of education and the right to equal opportunities for advancement regardless of race, religion or national origin.
Having this in mind, Mr. Chairman, I think we should take the opportunity at this time to include in the bill of rights the right of the individual to social security and his entitlement to realize the economic, social and cultural activities indispensable for his dignity and the free development of his personality. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Essex East:
That clause 1 be amended as follows:
That the following paragraph, to be designated paragraph (c), be added after the present paragraph (b):
"The right of the individual to social security and his entitlement to realize the economic, social and cultural activities indispensable for his dignity and the free development of his personality." and that the remaining paragraphs be relettered accordingly.

I am surprised and disappointed that the minister is not in a position to give sympathetic consideration to the inclusion of this amendment, and amendments of this type in the bill of rights. His argument against them, and we heard it earlier in the evening, was that they dealt with social and economic rights which are desirable, he says, as an objective, but not appropriate for inclusion in a bill of this kind.
This is the general attitude, I take it, which he takes toward amendments of this nature. My surprise at that attitude results from the fact that when the Prime Minister discussed this subject on May 16, 1947, he discussed what he would put in a bill of rights and he dealt with this particular matter. He first pointed out that he would set up a committee-this was in 1947-which would include representatives from the various provinces. This committee would act in cooperation with the provinces. Then he dealt with, and I am quoting again from page 3152 of Hansard for 1947, the political rights that he would include in his proposed bill. This was to be a bill of particulars of the political rights that would be included and which would be worked out in co-operation with the provinces. I quote the Prime Minister, who went on to say this:
Those were the political freedoms that I would have placed in a bill of rights. In addition to those, there would, of course, be social freedoms, if I may call them such,.-
What kind of social freedoms? The Prime Minister explained what he had in mind:
-assuring educational, property and social security rights.
This is what we are requesting. This afternoon the Prime Minister said that this bill included all that he had worked for for 14 years, so I am asking the minister now to help out the Prime Minister and put this kind of amendment in this bill so that the Prime Minister's words of this afternoon will be implemented, at least to this extent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister

Mr. Chairman, it is very interesting to watch the actions of the opposition on this occasion. For the last 15 years they have consistently opposed any bill of rights. They did everything possible to ridicule, disparage any action in this regard. Indeed as late as 1958 they were still in the same position. I sat here today and listened to this vast transformation, this
Human Rights
complete conversion, which is something that has resulted from the fact that public opinion has placed them in a position where, in order to secure forgiveness for their years of opposition, they now indulge in a conversion that would bring into existence every declaration that has ever been made, including the universal declaration of human rights which received the support of the United Nations but which they would not bring before parliament, not under any circumstances.
When we asked them over and over again to bring the universal declaration of human rights before parliament these protectors of the rights of the provinces, which they had transgressed so often, said we cannot do this; if we were to bring the universal declaration of human rights before parliament, we would be invading provincial jurisdiction. The Leader of the Opposition cannot get away from those words I read earlier, and which I shall read once more, uttered on September 5, 1958. There was an interruption on my part, which is as follows:
I do not want to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but he has brought up something there that only he can answer. Having accepted the universal declaration of human rights in the United Nations which, I think I am right in saying, was submitted by most other democratic countries in the world to their respective legislatures, why was that declaration of human freedoms not submitted to the parliament of Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was simply referring to the fact that these various articles in the universal declaration of human rights, which were regarded as improper to be brought before the House of Commons because they would infringe on provincial rights and would require the consent of the provinces before they could be brought before parliament, are now brought forward by the opposition.
I shall not refer to the sections further because I do not want to arouse the hon. gentlemen. They realize that one after the other has been taken holus-bolus in certain cases, in other cases abstracted from this universal declaration of human rights which they allowed to remain in abeyance, indeed refused to bring before parliament, through all the years that they were in power from 1948 to 1957. Now suddenly when we bring before the House of Commons a bill of rights these particular sections which were so detrimental to the constitutional background of Canada, and therefore improper to be dealt with in parliament, become the cornerstone of their argument. The series of amendments which were introduced in every case but one were included in this universal declaration to which I have referred in some particular.
Mr. Chairman, death bed repentances always lead to forgiveness. Here they are after all those years, having done everything they could conceivably do year after year to deny Canadians a bill of rights, now endeavouring to place themselves in the position of being the custodian of these rights which for so long they have denied Canadians.
I will say no more for the moment about that matter. It has been over and over again
Human Rights
the same course of action. Hon. members opposite started off by saying that the bill of rights contained nothing which would be beneficial. Others argued that the result would be uncertainty and a great deal of litigation because the effect would be that existing statutes which deny these principles would be interfered with or abrogated or indeed repealed. Alternatively they argued that the effect would be that any judge interpreting existing statutes which deny these freedoms will from now on be required to look at this bill of rights and, in the light of the fact that it declares that these fundamental freedoms have always existed, will interpret statutes now existing as though this particular bill of rights and its principles had always been on the statute books of this country.
I can see a great deal of interpretation that will come before the courts. I am not going to detail this unless I am put in a position that anyone demands to know the number of times that these fundamental freedoms were abrogated, diminished, trodden down during the period between 1945 and 1952. I simply say this: the purpose of this bill of rights is to secure for Canadians those things that are of the essence of freedom and within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. Several of the matters which were brought before the committee by way of amendments are matters which peculiarly fall within the jurisdiction of the provinces. My hope is that with regard to these questions which are within provincial jurisdiction, an agreement may be worked out which ultimately will achieve a bill of rights which will bring into existence those additional freedoms that peculiarly arise within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures, or which are in part matters of federal and provincial jurisdiction.

I return to the amendment and the amendment concerns the right of the individual to social security and his entitlement to realize the economic, social and cultural activities indispensable to his dignity and the free development of his personality. Those words are very similar to article 22 of the universal declaration. Indeed, when hon. gentlemen opposite talk about clothing these freedoms in grandiloquent language I would point out that article 22 succeeds rather better in that connection than the amendment. Article 22 reads as follows:
Everyone, as a member of society has the right to social security and is entitled to realization, through national effort and international co-operation and in accordance with the organization and resources of each state of the organization and and cultural rights indispensable for his dignity and the free development of his personality.
That was one of those rights which a few years ago could not be brought in in a declaration before parliament because of the fact

that a portion of that declaration comes within provincial jurisdiction. That is why I point out that one after another of these amendments, in the array in which they have been produced, fall singularly within provincial jurisdiction. I raise that in addition to the points made by the Minister of Justice.
In so far as securing provincial agreement to these things is concerned, when we do and if we do then indeed it will be possible to have a bill of rights which will achieve, not only political rights under the jurisdiction of the national government but political and social matters within the jurisdiction of both. When I hear it said over and over again how easy it would be to attain the objective of provincial consent to a bill of rights, may I point out that the Leader of the Opposition on September 5, 1958 when he was not sure whether he was going to be in favour of a bill of rights or against a bill of rights-

He brought the matter up again in 1952 with a draft bill which could be used for this purpose.
